Useful phrases: "You say this when...", "What if we chose...?", "Fair enough, but..." Write a short paragraph: your idioms, how you chose them, how the explanations worked and which idiom was hardest to explain.
quests.teacherNote: Strong pairs justify their choices and give situations, not translations. Other idioms: under the weather, hit the books, once in a blue moon, cost an arm and a leg.

quests.title: Invention Pitch
quests.text: Choose an ordinary object and present it in nearby chat as an amazing new invention, without naming it: "Tired of wet hair on rainy days? This light, foldable device..." Classmates must guess the object. Then answer their doubts and try to convince at least 4 of them that they can't live without it. Useful phrases: "Imagine never having to...", "Unlike other products, this...", "I see your point, but..." Write a short paragraph: your pitch, the doubts people raised, how you answered them, and how many classmates you convinced.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive structures and polite counter-arguments. Funny everyday choices (a spoon, a sock, a stapler) make the best pitches. The example in the text is an umbrella.

quests.title: Alien Field Report
quests.text: Imagine you are an alien scientist studying humans in Pixel Plaza. Invent three strange but accurate descriptions of human objects or habits without naming them, for example: "Every morning, humans pour white liquid from a large animal onto small dry pieces, then eat them with a metal tool." Post them one at a time in nearby chat and see which classmates can decode them. Avoid obvious key words. Useful phrases: "a device that...", "a ritual in which..." Write a short paragraph: your descriptions, what classmates guessed, and which one was hardest to decode and why.
quests.teacherNote: The example is breakfast cereal with milk. Reward precise, funny paraphrasing (a phone is "a glowing rectangle humans stare at") and check that the key words are avoided.

quests.title: Explain the Invisible
quests.text: Take turns with 2-3 classmates: describe something you cannot see or touch, without naming it (a natural force, a sound, a technology or an idea). The others guess. Do at least two rounds each. Then rank the things from hardest to easiest to describe and agree on one group ranking. Useful phrases: "It's tricky to describe because...", "I'd put... above... since...", "Let's compromise:..." Write a short paragraph: your ranking, the different views in your group and how you reached agreement.
quests.teacherNote: If a group gets stuck, suggest wind, Wi-Fi, time, gravity, an echo or a secret. Listen for rankings with reasons and for compromise language.

quests.title: Operation Pizza
quests.text: Make a classmate write the secret word "pizza". You cannot write it first! Ask food questions: "What food do you like?" Then write: "... says pizza when I ask about ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check that the student asked real questions (What do you eat on Fridays? What food is from Italy?) and did not just tell the classmate to write the word. If pizza is too hard, let them choose another food word.

quests.title: Colour Twin Hunt
quests.text: Find your colour twin! Ask four classmates: "What is your favourite colour?" Find someone with the same favourite colour as you. Write: "My favourite colour is ... and ... likes it too."
quests.teacherNote: If nobody has the same colour, the student can write the closest match (light blue and dark blue). Encourage students to answer everyone who asks them, so the whole class practises.

quests.title: Bridge Code Guards
quests.text: Choose an English code word with two classmates. Stand on the bridge. Ask everyone: "Can you guess our code word?" Give clues: "It is green." Write: "Our code word is ... and ... guesses it."
quests.teacherNote: Look for short clue sentences like "It is big" or "It can fly". If nobody guesses, the student writes "nobody guesses it" and the mission still counts as done.

quests.title: Crack the Number Code
quests.text: Crack the code: A=1, B=2, C=3 and so on. The agent's favourite food is 3-1-11-5. Type the food. Then send a number code to a classmate: "Can you read 4-15-7?"
quests.teacherNote: Solution: 3-1-11-5 is C-A-K-E, so the answer is cake. Fast finishers can swap number codes with classmates (4-15-7 is dog).

quests.title: Agent Name Maker
quests.text: Give a classmate an agent name from their avatar, like "Agent Red Hat". Send it and ask: "Do you like it?" They name you too. Write: "I am Agent ... and ... is Agent ..."
quests.teacherNote: Names must be friendly and based only on the avatar's colours and clothes (hat, glasses, shirt, hair colour). If a classmate does not like their name, they choose a new one together.

quests.title: Evening Spy Report
quests.text: Be a past-time spy! Ask two classmates: "What did you do yesterday evening?" Then ask one more question about each answer, like "Did you like it?" Useful phrases: "I watched...", "I went to...", "Did you...?" Write 2-3 sentences: what each classmate did and what you asked next. Share only what you want.
quests.teacherNote: Look for past simple questions and answers (Did you...? I played...) and a real follow-up question. Remind students that nobody has to share anything private; they can invent a fun answer.

quests.title: Word Smuggler
quests.text: Chat with two or three classmates in nearby chat. Secretly use these words in normal sentences: umbrella, dinosaur, sandwich. Example: "I saw a dinosaur film last week." Then ask: "Can you guess my three secret words?" Write 2-3 sentences: how you used them and who guessed.
quests.teacherNote: Praise sentences that fit naturally into the conversation, because hiding the words is the real challenge. You can swap the three words for vocabulary from the current story chapter.

quests.title: Secret Meeting Plan
quests.text: Plan a secret meeting with a classmate. Where and when are you going to meet? Invent a code question and answer, like "Is the cafe open?" - "Only for ducks." Then meet there and test it! Useful phrases: "Let's meet at...", "We're going to..." Write 3 sentences about your plan.
quests.teacherNote: Check for "going to" and suggestions (Let's..., How about...?). Encourage the pair to really meet at the place and try their code question and answer.

quests.title: Undercover Object
quests.text: Choose a secret thing in Pixel Plaza, like a bench, a cup of coffee or a duck. Tell four classmates: "I'm a secret thing. Ask me yes/no questions!" Useful questions: "Are you in the park?", "Can people eat you?" Write 2-3 sentences: what you chose, who guessed and how many questions they asked. During the round, the clue-giver answers yes or no without naming the object. Guessers may name their guesses; confirm a correct guess with yes.
quests.teacherNote: Check question forms (Are you...? Can you...? Is it...?). Students can choose a new secret thing for each classmate to keep the game fresh. Student-chosen secrets are not registered in the app, so these round rules need teacher review; there is no automatic word block for this quest.

quests.title: First Letter Secret
quests.text: Read the secret message: "Funny Old Uncles Never Tell Anyone Interesting News." The first letters of the words spell the meeting place. Type the place. Then hide a word in a sentence like this and send it to a classmate. Can they find it?
quests.teacherNote: Solution: the first letters spell F-O-U-N-T-A-I-N, so the answer is fountain. Writing their own hidden-word sentences is good extra vocabulary practice.

quests.title: Spot the Double Agent
quests.text: Tell two or three classmates three facts about yourself: two true, one a lie. Choose safe topics like hobbies, food or places you have visited. The group asks follow-up questions to find the lie, and you defend it. Then swap roles. Useful phrases: "When did you...?", "I think it's a lie because..." Write 3-5 sentences: your facts, the best questions and who found your lie.
quests.teacherNote: Remind students to use facts about themselves only and nothing private (no addresses, family problems, etc.). Look for follow-up questions in the past simple and present perfect.

quests.title: Common Ground Mission
quests.text: Find something surprising you have in common with four different classmates, ideally people you don't often talk to. Obvious things like "We both like pizza" don't count! Ask follow-up questions to go deeper. Useful phrases: "Me too! What about...?", "Have you ever...?", "Really? Which one?" Write 3-5 sentences: who you talked to and what you have in common.
quests.teacherNote: Strong answers go beyond food and colours (both collect something, both can't whistle, both have been to the same beach). Watch that nobody is left out, and pair up students who are still looking.

quests.title: Gadget Lab
quests.text: Invent a helpful spy gadget made from an everyday object, like a pen or an umbrella. Describe it to a classmate without naming the object: can they guess it? Then ask about their gadget and decide together which one is more useful and why. Useful phrases: "It's used for...", "It can...", "... is more useful than... because..." Write 3-5 sentences about both gadgets and your decision.
quests.teacherNote: Look for "is used for" and comparatives with reasons. Keep gadgets helpful and harmless (no weapons).

quests.title: Who Has the Key
quests.text: Solve the mystery: four agents are at the cafe, but only one has the secret key. Agent Owl is the youngest. Agent Bear is older than Agent Fox. Agent Cat is younger than Agent Fox. The agent with the key is older than Agent Cat but isn't the oldest. Who has the key? Type the agent's name. Then explain your reasoning to a classmate. Useful phrases: "It can't be... because...", "So it must be..."
quests.teacherNote: Solution: from youngest to oldest the order is Owl, Cat, Fox, Bear, so the agent who is older than Cat but not the oldest is Fox. Ask students to justify it, e.g. "It can't be Bear because Bear is the oldest".

quests.title: Pass It On, Agent
quests.text: Start a top-secret relay with two or three classmates and explain the rules first. Send this message to the first agent: "The golden duck will meet you near the fountain after lunch, so bring a sandwich." Each agent passes it on in their own words, without copying. The last agent sends it back to you. Useful phrases: "In other words...", "It means that..." Write 3-5 sentences: how the message changed and which version you prefer.
quests.teacherNote: Good paraphrases keep the meaning but change the words ("after lunch" becomes "in the afternoon"). For weaker groups, let each agent change only two or three words.

quests.title: Mind Changer Mission
quests.text: Pick a light opinion, for example "Summer is better than winter" or "Cats make better pets than dogs". Try to change the minds of four classmates who disagree or are not sure. Give reasons, answer their objections and ask: "What would change your mind?" Never push anyone; polite disagreement is fine. Useful phrases: "Have you considered...?", "That's a fair point, but...", "I'd be more convinced if..." Write a short paragraph: your opinion, your best arguments, who changed their mind and why, and what you would do differently.
quests.teacherNote: Look for counter-arguments and hedging (That's a fair point, but...). Keep topics light; ban religion, party politics and anything about real people.

quests.title: Undercover Opinion Poll
quests.text: Find out what four classmates think about this question without asking it directly: "Should school start an hour later?" Instead, chat about mornings, sleep, after-school activities and free time, and guess each person's opinion. At the end, reveal your mission and check whether you were right. Useful phrases: "How do you feel about...?", "Would you rather...?" Write a short paragraph summarising the different views, including any "yes, but..." answers, and how accurate your guesses were.
quests.teacherNote: Look for summarising language (Most people..., While X thinks..., Y was less sure because...). You can swap the topic for any current class debate, such as homework at weekends.

quests.title: The Golden Duck Alibi
quests.text: Investigate the case of the missing golden duck statue, which vanished from the fountain yesterday between 4 and 5 pm. In a group of three, two classmates are the suspects: give them two minutes to invent a detailed alibi together (where they were and what they did). You are the detective. Send questions to each suspect separately, such as "What exactly did you order?" or "What was the weather like?", and compare their answers. Any difference means the alibi has a hole! It is only a game. Write a short paragraph explaining which details matched, which didn't, and your final verdict.
quests.teacherNote: Look for past continuous and past simple (What were you doing at 4.30? What did you order?) and precise follow-up questions. Rotate roles so everyone gets to be the detective, and keep the tone playful.

quests.title: Spy Dilemma Debate
quests.text: Discuss three spy dilemmas with a classmate and try to agree on the best plan for each. One: what would you do if you found a secret map under a park bench? Two: if your code phrase were discovered, how would you warn your team? Three: would you rather have an invisibility gadget or a flying one, and why? Useful phrases: "If I were you, I'd...", "That might work, but..." Write a short paragraph summarising both opinions and what you agreed on.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for the second conditional and polite disagreement. Pairs who finish early can invent a fourth dilemma for another pair.

quests.title: Secret HQ Showdown
quests.text: Choose the perfect secret headquarters for your spy team. With two or three classmates, each agent argues for a different place in Pixel Plaza: the hotel, the cafe, the shop or the park. Give convincing reasons (hidden corners, a good view, easy escape, snacks) and answer the others' arguments. You must reach one decision together, so be ready to compromise. Useful phrases: "I see your point, but...", "What if we...?", "Wouldn't it be better to...?" Write a short paragraph summarising each agent's argument, the final decision and why it won.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive language and real compromise (the cafe by day, the park at night). If the group agrees too quickly, ask each student to argue for a place they did not pick first.

quests.title: Our Class Pet
quests.text: Choose a class pet with a classmate: a cat, a fish, a rabbit or a hamster. Ask: "Do you like cats?" Agree on one pet. Write: "Our class pet is a ... because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check in the chat log that the pair asked at least one question before agreeing. For a challenge, ask them to add a name for the pet.

quests.title: Season Vote
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates: "What is the best season: spring, summer, autumn or winter?" Count the votes. Write: "The winner is ... with ... votes."
quests.teacherNote: Students can stand in the square and ask in nearby chat. If there is a tie, they can ask one more classmate or write "It is a draw." (Replaced the party-place vote, which duplicated the B2 party quest.)

quests.title: Square Game
quests.text: Choose a game for the square with 2 or 3 classmates: tag, hide and seek, or a quiz. Ask: "Do you want to play tag?" Say yes or no. Write: "We play ... in the square because it is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Any choice is fine; the point is that the group asks and answers before deciding. Faster groups can add a second game and say which one is better. (Replaced Island Bag, which duplicated the B1 desert island quest.)

quests.title: Picnic by the Pond
quests.text: Meet a classmate at the pond and plan a picnic. Say "I like ..." or "I don't like ...". Choose 3 foods together. Write: "We take ..., ... and ... to the picnic."
quests.teacherNote: Look for "I like / I don't like" in the chat before the decision. Stronger students can add one drink and one game for the picnic.

quests.title: The Oldest Invention
quests.text: Guess the oldest invention: the phone, the wheel or the computer. Ask a classmate: "What do you think?" Then type the oldest one.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the wheel (about 5,500 years old); the phone is from the 1870s and the computer from the 20th century. Extend it by asking students to rank all three in the chat.

quests.title: Rainy Day Plan (Team Decisions)
quests.text: Plan a rainy day in Pixel Plaza with 2 or 3 classmates. Choose a place (the cafe, the hotel or the shop) and two activities. Useful phrases: "Let's go to ...", "What about ...?", "Good idea!" Write 3 sentences: where you are going to go, what you are going to do and why.
quests.teacherNote: Check that the sentences use "going to". If the group cannot agree, they can vote and mention the vote in their answer. (Replaced Class Trip Plan, which duplicated the B2 trip quest.)

quests.title: Playlist Vote
quests.text: Choose music for a class playlist. Suggest a type of music in nearby chat. Then ask 4 classmates: "Which music do you vote for?" Useful phrases: "I vote for ...", "It's fun/calm/great for dancing." Write 3 sentences: which types people suggested, how many votes each one got and which one won.
quests.teacherNote: Look for past simple forms (suggested, got, won) in the answers. Kind comments only: nobody's taste is wrong. (Replaced the mascot vote, which was too close to the class pet and the mascot puzzle.)

quests.title: Lunch Menu Ranking
quests.text: Rank these school lunches from 1 (best) to 5 (worst): pasta, fish, salad, pizza, soup. Compare with a classmate and make one list together. Useful phrases: "My number one is ...", "I agree.", "I don't agree because ..." Write 3 sentences: your number one, your number five and one thing you disagreed about.
quests.teacherNote: Pairs should agree on one shared list, not just report two separate lists. You can swap the foods for local favourites.

quests.title: Sports Day Vote
quests.text: Read the clues. Your class voted for one sport for sports day. Basketball got more votes than tennis. Volleyball got fewer votes than tennis. Football got the most votes. Which sport came last? Check with a classmate, then type the sport.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: volleyball (order: football, basketball, tennis, volleyball). Early finishers can write their own vote puzzle and whisper it to a classmate.

quests.title: Class Superpower
quests.text: Agree on ONE superpower for your whole class with a classmate: flying, being invisible, speaking every language or stopping time. Useful phrases: "I think ... is better because ...", "OK, let's choose ..." Write 3 sentences: your choice, one reason, and one thing the class is going to do with it.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage pairs to compare the options ("better than", "more useful than") before deciding. Funny ideas are welcome as long as they are kind.

quests.title: Invention Top Three
quests.text: Rank these inventions from most to least important: the wheel, the fridge, the bicycle, the internet, the toothbrush. Then compare your list with a classmate and agree on a shared top three. Ask follow-up questions, e.g. "Why is that more important than the bicycle?" Useful phrases: "I'd put ... first because ...", "... is more useful than ...", "Fair point, but ..." Write 4 sentences: your shared top three, the best reason you heard and one thing you disagreed about.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for comparatives and real reasons, not just a list. To reuse it, swap in other inventions (the phone, glasses, the washing machine).

quests.title: Desert Island Survival
quests.text: Imagine your boat is stuck on a desert island for one week. You can keep only 4 of these: a rope, a mirror, a tent, matches, sunscreen, a fishing net, a guitar, a cooking pot. Discuss with 2 or 3 classmates and agree on your 4. Useful phrases: "We need ... because ...", "... is more useful than ...", "What if it rains?" Write 4-5 sentences: your 4 items, why you chose them and one item you were sad to leave.
quests.teacherNote: There is no single right answer; good groups explain how they would use each item (the mirror for signalling, the pot for boiling water). If there is time, groups can compare lists with another group.

quests.title: Plaza Upgrade
quests.text: Find out what your town needs. Pixel Plaza can build ONE new place: a skate park, a cinema, a swimming pool or a library. Ask at least 4 classmates which one they prefer and why. Ask a follow-up question, e.g. "How often would you go there?" Useful phrases: "Which would you prefer?", "Most people think ...", "Only one person ..." Write 4-5 sentences: the most popular choice, the best reason you heard and your own opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Look for reported results ("Three people prefer...") and a personal opinion with a reason. You can change the four options to match a unit topic.

quests.title: New Class Rule
quests.text: Agree on ONE new fun rule for your class with 2 or 3 classmates. Everyone suggests one idea, for example music while you work, a joke every Friday, or a five-minute break after a test. Compare the ideas and choose the best one. Useful phrases: "That would be fun, but ...", "I prefer ... because ...", "Shall we vote?" Write 4 sentences: everyone's ideas, the winner and why you chose it.
quests.teacherNote: The rule should be kind and realistic; you could even try the winning rule for a week. Listen for "would" and comparisons while they choose.

quests.title: Club Puzzle
quests.text: Solve the puzzle. Four friends each joined a different club: chess, drama, football or art. Ana did not join football or art. Ben did not join chess or art. Cleo did not join chess, drama or art. Who joined the art club? Compare your answer with a classmate, then type the name.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Dan. Cleo must be football; then Ben is drama, Ana is chess, so Dan is art. Ask students to explain their steps to a classmate in the chat. (Replaced the mascot ranking puzzle, which repeated the A2 ranking puzzle.)

quests.title: Balloon Debate
quests.text: Imagine a hot-air balloon is sinking and carries four places from Pixel Plaza: the cafe, the shop, the hotel and the park. Each person in your group of 3 or 4 defends one place (with three people, leave out the shop). Explain why the town would be worse without it. Then negotiate which place goes overboard first, then second, until only one is left. Useful phrases: "Without ..., we wouldn't be able to ...", "I see your point, but ...", "If we lost ..., ..." Write a short paragraph: which place survived, the strongest argument you heard and whether anyone changed your mind.
quests.teacherNote: Look for conditional arguments ("If we didn't have...") and polite disagreement. Only places are thrown out, never people or avatars. (Changed from inventions to Plaza places to avoid repeating the B1 inventions quest.)

quests.title: Trip on a Budget
quests.text: Plan a three-day class trip with a classmate. You have 100 points (not real money). Transport: train 30 or bus 15. Sleeping: hotel 50, youth hostel 30 or camping 10. Activities: theme park 40, kayaking 25, cooking class 20, museum 10. Negotiate so that each of you gets at least one thing you really want. Useful phrases: "If we take the bus, we could afford ...", "I'd accept ... as long as ...", "How about a compromise?" Write a short paragraph: your final plan, what each of you gave up and why it is fair.
quests.teacherNote: Check that the plan costs 100 points or less and that the paragraph explains the compromise, not just the choices. Change the prices to make it harder.

quests.title: Party Theme Summit
quests.text: Help your class choose a theme for an end-of-term party (or another celebration you like): 80s disco, video games, beach party or superheroes. Talk to at least 5 classmates, ask which theme they prefer and what would make it fun for everyone. Note where people agree and disagree. Then propose a compromise that keeps most people happy, such as mixing two themes. Useful phrases: "Most people seem to ...", "On the other hand, ...", "What if we combined ...?" Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and your final proposal.
quests.teacherNote: A strong answer reports several views ("Some people..., while others...") before making a proposal. If a real class event is coming up, use it instead.

quests.title: Museum of Today
quests.text: Imagine a museum in 100 years wants three everyday objects to show how teenagers live today. With 2 or 3 classmates, suggest objects, then negotiate a final list of three. For each one, agree on what it would tell future visitors about life today. Useful phrases: "People in the future might think ...", "That says a lot about ...", "I'd swap ... for ... because ..." Write a short paragraph: your three objects, what each one shows and one object you argued about.
quests.teacherNote: Push for reasons beyond "it's popular": what the object shows about habits, values or technology. It works well before a unit on the past or the future.

quests.title: Robot Helper Deal
quests.text: Imagine your school gets one robot, but it can only do three jobs: clean the classrooms, serve lunch, carry heavy bags, help with homework, translate for new students or organise the library. Choose your three alone first, then negotiate one shared list with a classmate. Discuss the downsides too: "If the robot helped with homework, would we learn less?" Useful phrases: "The main advantage is ...", "The problem with that is ...", "Fair enough, I'll give up ... if ..." Write a short paragraph: your final three jobs, why, and one disadvantage you discussed.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for second conditionals and arguments that weigh both sides. Fast pairs can rank all six jobs.

quests.title: Nice Avatar
quests.text: Find a classmate. Say one nice thing about their avatar. Use: "I like your ... because ...". Write 2 sentences: what you say and what your classmate says.
quests.teacherNote: Look for a real reason after 'because' (colour, style, hat). Model a polite reply such as 'Thank you!' for students who stay silent.

quests.title: Thank You Message
quests.text: Send a thank you to a classmate. Use: "Thank you for your ...". Ideas: help, smile, joke. Write 2 sentences: what you say and what your classmate says.
quests.teacherNote: A quick warm-up. Check that students use 'for your' + noun and that the classmate replies (for example 'You are welcome').

quests.title: Welcome to Pixel Plaza
quests.text: Pretend four classmates are new in town. Say to each one: "Welcome to Pixel Plaza! The ... is nice." Use cafe, shop, park or hotel. Write 2 sentences: which places you tell them about.
quests.teacherNote: Students practise place vocabulary and a friendly greeting. Encourage them to choose a different place for each classmate.

quests.title: Shirt Compliments
quests.text: Find four classmates with different shirts. Say "I like your shirt!" Ask "What is your favourite colour?" Write 2 sentences about two answers: "... likes ...".
quests.teacherNote: Check 'likes' with the third person -s. Students can use any name shown above an avatar.

quests.title: Cheer Up Cards
quests.text: Imagine a friend is sad. Write 2 kind sentences for them. Use: "Don't worry! You are ..." and "I am here for you." Then send one sentence to a classmate.
quests.teacherNote: Accept any positive adjective (strong, funny, kind). Whispering one sentence is optional extra practice for fast finishers.

quests.title: Compliment Chain
quests.text: Meet three classmates. Person 1 compliments Person 2's avatar. Person 2 says thanks and compliments Person 3. Continue until everyone gets a compliment. Useful phrases: "Your ... looks great." "That is a cool ...". Write 3 sentences: what you heard and what you said.
quests.teacherNote: Compliments should be about avatars only. Encourage students to avoid repeating the same adjective.

quests.title: Tip Swap
quests.text: Ask a classmate for a tip about the game, for example how to find the park fast. Then give them a tip too. Useful phrases: "Can you give me a tip?" "You should ..." "Thanks, that helps!" Write 3 sentences: the tips you gave and got.
quests.teacherNote: Look for 'should' plus a base verb and a thank-you at the end. Tips can be about movement, chat or any part of Pixel Plaza.

quests.title: Kind Moment Survey
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "What kind thing did someone do for you last week?" Choose a small, happy thing at school. Reply "That is lovely!" Write 3 sentences about their answers, for example: "One classmate said a friend helped with homework."
quests.teacherNote: Remind students to keep answers light and school-related; they may invent an example. Check past simple forms such as helped, shared, gave.

quests.title: Welcome Tour Plan
quests.text: Plan a welcome tour for a new student. With two or three classmates, choose three places in Pixel Plaza. Say what the new student is going to do there. Useful phrases: "First, we are going to ..." "Then ..." Write 3 sentences with your plan.
quests.teacherNote: Check 'be going to' and the sequencing words first, then, finally. Places: hotel, cafe, shop, fountain square, park, pond, bridge.

quests.title: Helping Hands
quests.text: Ask a classmate for help with a small pretend job, like carrying boxes to the shop or finding a hat in the park. Useful phrases: "Can you help me?" "Of course! I can ..." "Thank you so much!" Swap roles with a new job. Write 3 sentences: the jobs and who helped.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for polite requests (Can/Could you ...?) and friendly offers. Jobs are invented, so nobody shares anything personal.

quests.title: Compliment Detective
quests.text: Ask four classmates which compliment feels best: about their avatar, their ideas, their helping, or their jokes. Ask a follow-up question: "Why does that one feel best?" Compare the answers. Useful phrases: "The most popular was ..." "Most people said ... because ..." "In contrast, ..." Write 4 sentences summarising what you found.
quests.teacherNote: Look for reasons and summary language. Fast students can note which type of compliment nobody chose.

quests.title: Kind Action Plan
quests.text: With three classmates, talk about three small situations: a new player stands alone at the fountain, a player loses a mini-game, a player cannot find the cafe. For each one, suggest a kind action and give a reason. Useful phrases: "We could ... because ..." "Why don't we ...?" "I agree, so ..." Write 4 sentences: your best idea for each situation and one thing your group agreed on.
quests.teacherNote: Check that everyone suggests something with a reason. Groups can add their own situation if they finish early.

quests.title: Advice Column
quests.text: Write a pretend problem letter, such as "I want to join a team but I am shy." Send it to a classmate. They reply with advice and a reason. Then swap. Useful phrases: "If I were you, I would ..." "It might help to ..." Write 4 sentences: the problem and the best advice you got.
quests.teacherNote: Problems must be invented and light. Praise 'If I were you, I would ...' and advice that comes with a reason.

quests.title: Gratitude Round
quests.text: With two or three classmates, take turns saying one thing at school or in town you are thankful for, and why. After each person, ask a follow-up question. Useful phrases: "I am really grateful for ... because ..." "What do you like most about it?" Write 4 sentences: what people were thankful for and one surprising answer.
quests.teacherNote: Keep topics light (a club, a teacher's help, a place). Check that follow-up questions are real questions and not only 'Why?'.

quests.title: Honest or Kind
quests.text: Discuss with a classmate: is it okay to say "I love it!" about a friend's idea when you do not really like it? Give your opinion with two reasons and ask what they think. Find one kind AND honest way to answer. Useful phrases: "In my opinion ..." "On the one hand ..." "A better way to say it is ..." Write 4 sentences: your opinions and your kind, honest sentence.
quests.teacherNote: Students practise tactful feedback. Look for contrast linkers and a sentence like 'I like the colours, but maybe we could ...'.

quests.title: Kindness Week Vote
quests.text: In a group of four, imagine Pixel Plaza is starting a Kindness Week and you can run only one project: a thank-you wall, a buddy system for newcomers, a compliment booth in the cafe, or a helpers' club. Each person argues for a different project. Listen, question each other, then negotiate and vote. Write a short paragraph: the options, the strongest argument you heard, the winner, and why you accepted it, even if it was not your first choice.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive structures, concessions ('I see your point, but ...') and a genuine compromise. Groups of three can drop one option.

quests.title: Effort or Talent
quests.text: Ask at least four classmates: is it better to compliment someone's effort or their talent, and why? Challenge one answer politely, for example "But what if ...?" Summarise the different views, saying who agreed and who disagreed (say "one classmate" or use initials). Write a short paragraph with your conclusion and one example of a really good compliment.
quests.teacherNote: Check for reported speech, balanced summary and a clear conclusion. The best compliments usually name something specific.

quests.title: Lazy Teammate Dilemma
quests.text: Imagine your group project is due tomorrow and one imaginary teammate has done nothing. With two or three classmates, discuss what you would do and what might happen with each option: talk to them privately, ask the teacher, do their part, or change the plan. Reach an agreement that is fair and kind. Write a short paragraph: the options, the consequences you discussed, and your final plan.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for second and third conditionals. The situation is invented, so remind students not to name real classmates.

quests.title: Newcomer Charter
quests.text: Imagine a new student joins your class tomorrow and does not speak much English. With a group, design a three-point welcome plan that makes them feel included without putting them in the spotlight. Negotiate the wording of each point. Write a short paragraph: your three points, one disagreement you solved, and why you think the plan would work.
quests.teacherNote: Look for sensitive ideas such as a buddy, simple instructions, or optional participation. Check for modals (could, should, might) and justified choices.

quests.title: Speech Workshop
quests.text: Plan a short thank-you speech of about five sentences for an invented person who helped you in a tough moment, for example a coach who believed in you. Send it to a classmate in the chat. They give one compliment and one suggestion to make it warmer. Swap roles. Write a short paragraph: summarise your speech, the feedback you got, and how you would improve it.
quests.teacherNote: The helper must be invented to avoid personal stories. Look for varied gratitude vocabulary and specific, kind feedback.

quests.title: Hobby Hunt
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "What do you do in your free time?" Then write 2 sentences with their answers: "She likes ... ." "He plays ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Look for third-person -s (likes, plays). Good warm-up; students can reuse the same sentence frame for each answer.

quests.title: Sport Match
quests.text: Ask a classmate: "Do you like football? Do you like swimming?" Ask about two more sports. Find one sport you both like. Write: "We both like ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Practises yes/no questions and short answers (Yes, I do / No, I don't). If no sport matches, students write about the closest one.

quests.title: Saturday Clock
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "What time do you get up on Saturday?" Write 2 sentences: "I get up at ... on Saturday." "She gets up at ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Check the time expressions (at eight, at ten thirty) and -s for he/she. Replaced a task too similar to Hobby Hunt; keep answers free of personal details.

quests.title: Ball Game Riddle
quests.text: Read: Two teams play. A high net is between them. They hit a big ball with their hands. It cannot touch the floor. Ask a classmate for help. What sport is it? Type the sport.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: volleyball (two teams, high net, ball hit with hands, ball cannot touch the floor). Tennis and badminton use rackets; handball and basketball have no net between teams.

quests.title: Try Something New
quests.text: Choose a hobby you want to try. Tell a classmate and ask: "Do you want to try it too?" Then write: "I want to try ... because ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Look for want to + verb/noun and a simple reason with because. Encourage funny or unusual hobbies.

quests.title: Weekend News
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "What did you do last weekend?" Ask one more question, for example "Was it fun?" Useful phrases: "I played ...", "We went to ...". Write 3 sentences about what they did.
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple forms (went, played, watched). Weaker students can answer with one activity; stronger ones add a follow-up detail.

quests.title: Skill Swap
quests.text: Ask a classmate: "What can you do well?" Choose one easy skill, for example cooking an egg or juggling. Your partner explains how to do it. Useful phrases: "First, ...", "Then, ...". Write 3 sentences with the steps.
quests.teacherNote: Practises can and sequencing words. Remind students to choose harmless, simple skills; the steps can be about an imaginary activity.

quests.title: Perfect Saturday
quests.text: Plan a perfect Saturday with a classmate. Choose three places in Pixel Plaza, for example the cafe, the park and the square. Useful phrases: "Let's ...", "How about ...?". Write 3 sentences: "We are going to ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Look for Let's / How about and going to for plans. Students must agree, so listen for polite disagreement too.

quests.title: Board Game Clue
quests.text: Read the clues. This game has a board with 64 squares. Each player has 16 pieces. The most important piece is the king. Ask a classmate if you need help. What is the game? Type its name.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: chess (64 squares, 16 pieces each, the king is the key piece). Draughts/checkers also uses a 64-square board but each player has only 12 pieces.

quests.title: Class Sport Poll
quests.text: Find the most popular sport in your class. Ask five classmates: "What is your favourite sport?" Useful phrases: "Most people like ...", "Two people chose ...". Write 3 sentences with your results.
quests.teacherNote: Look for quantifiers (most, two, nobody) and accurate reporting. Compare totals as a class afterwards.

quests.title: Hobby Matchmaker
quests.text: Ask two classmates: "Do you prefer relaxing or active free time?" Then recommend one hobby or sport to each of them and give a reason. Ask a follow-up question. Useful phrases: "You might enjoy ... because ...", "Have you ever tried ...?", "That sounds ...". Write 4 sentences: what you recommended and how they reacted.
quests.teacherNote: Look for recommendation language with reasons and genuine follow-up questions. Students can choose imaginary hobbies if they have no ideas.

quests.title: Sport Showdown
quests.text: Choose two sports, for example basketball and swimming. With a classmate, compare them: which is more fun, harder, or better for teams? Useful phrases: "X is more ... than Y", "I agree, but ...", "On the other hand, ...". Write 4 sentences comparing the sports and say which one you chose together.
quests.teacherNote: Check comparative forms (more exciting than, easier than). Encourage reasons rather than just 'it is better'.

quests.title: Routine Detective
quests.text: Ask two classmates about their after-school routine: what they usually do and how often. Compare it with yours. Useful phrases: "How often do you ...?", "I usually ..., but she ...", "We both ...". Write 4 sentences about the differences and similarities.
quests.teacherNote: Look for frequency adverbs (usually, sometimes, never) and contrast linkers (but, while). Advise students to keep answers about activities, not private matters.

quests.title: Hobby Logic Puzzle
quests.text: Solve this puzzle with a classmate. Ana, Ben and Cleo have different hobbies: chess, skateboarding and painting. Ana never plays chess. Ana never uses a brush. Ben never uses wheels. Cleo never plays board games. Who plays chess? Useful phrases: "It can't be ...", "So it must be ...". Type one name.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: Ana skateboards (not chess, not painting), so Cleo paints (not chess) and Ben plays chess (not wheels). Encourage students to explain their reasoning in the chat.

quests.title: Club Makeover
quests.text: Invent a new free-time club, for example a pixel-art club or a park picnic club. Tell three classmates about it and ask: "What do you like about it? What could be better?" Improve your club with their ideas. Useful phrases: "You could ...", "I like the idea of ...", "Maybe you should ...". Write 4 sentences: your club, their opinions and your changes.
quests.teacherNote: Look for opinions with reasons and kind, constructive suggestions (could/should). Changed from a persuasion task to avoid overlap with the B2 Hobby Fair Pitch; students can vote on the best club afterwards.

quests.title: Is Gaming a Hobby
quests.text: Is playing video games a real hobby, or just a way to pass time? Ask two or three classmates for their views and try to hear at least one different opinion from yours. Respond politely to what they say. Useful phrases: "I see your point, but ...", "It depends on ...", "What do you mean by ...?". Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and say whether anyone changed your mind.
quests.teacherNote: Look for balanced summaries, reported views (she argued that ...) and polite disagreement. The topic is mild, but remind students to respect all opinions.

quests.title: Free Afternoon Deal
quests.text: Imagine your school gives your class one extra free afternoon every week. With a classmate, each of you suggests a different activity for the whole class, then you negotiate one final plan that works for both of you. Try to use if-sentences, for example "If we chose ..., everyone could ...". Write a short paragraph: both ideas, your compromise, and why it works.
quests.teacherNote: Look for compromise language, conditionals and persuasive reasons. Strong pairs may explain how the plan includes quieter and more active students.

quests.title: Overnight Master
quests.text: If you could master any sport, instrument or hobby overnight, with no practice, which one would you choose? Would it still be fun if you never had to learn it? Ask two classmates the same questions. Useful phrases: "If I could, I would ...", "On the one hand ..., on the other hand ...". Write a short paragraph comparing your answers and explaining who has the most interesting reason.
quests.teacherNote: Look for second conditional (would) and contrasting ideas about effort versus result. Good opening for a short class discussion about why learning can be part of the fun.

quests.title: Hobby Fair Pitch
quests.text: Convince three classmates to try a hobby you love. Prepare two strong reasons, then listen to their objections, such as "It sounds too difficult" or "I'd get bored", and answer them. Useful phrases: "You might think ..., but actually ...", "What if I told you ...?". Write a short paragraph: your hobby, your best arguments, the objections you heard, and who you convinced.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for persuasive structures and responses to objections, not just lists of reasons. Students may pitch a hobby they only like a little or invent one.

quests.title: Club Calendar Puzzle
quests.text: Three clubs all meet today. The chess club meets every 4 days, the dance club every 6 days and the debate club every 9 days. Work with a classmate and explain your reasoning in the chat, using "If ..., then ...". After how many days will all three clubs meet together again? Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: 36 days, the lowest common multiple of 4, 6 and 9 (4 and 6 alone give 12, but 12 is not a multiple of 9). Encourage students to list meeting days and explain in English.

quests.title: Favourite Song
quests.text: Ask a classmate: 'What is your favourite song? Why?' Then write 2 sentences: 'My classmate likes ... because ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Look for 'likes' with the third-person s and a simple reason. Remind students to keep song choices suitable for school.

quests.title: Game Fans
quests.text: Ask 3 classmates: 'Do you play video games?' Then write 2 sentences: '... classmates play games. My favourite game is ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Students practise 'Do you...?' and short answers. Students who do not play video games can write about board games or sports.

quests.title: Film Friends
quests.text: Ask a classmate: 'Do you like comedy films? Do you like cartoons?' Then write 2 sentences: 'We both like ...' or 'I like ... but my classmate likes ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Check 'like' versus 'likes' and short answers (Yes, I do / No, I don't). Students can swap in other genres such as action or horror-lite.

quests.title: Music Mood
quests.text: Choose one kind of music: pop, rock, rap, or another. Tell a classmate: 'I like ... music.' Ask: 'Do you like it?' Write 2 sentences: 'I like ... music because it is ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Adjectives like fun, loud, slow, happy are good. Accept any genre.

quests.title: Series Match
quests.text: Name a TV series you like. Ask 4 classmates: 'Do you like ...?' Write 2 sentences: 'My series is ... ' and '... classmates like it.'
quests.teacherNote: Students find who shares their taste. If nobody likes it, '0 classmates like it' is a fine result; encourage a second question about another series.

quests.title: Yellow Ghost Runner
quests.text: Solve the riddle. I am yellow. I live in a video game. I eat dots and I run away from four ghosts. Who am I? Ask a classmate to guess too. Then type my name.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: Pac-Man, the classic arcade character. Students can then make their own riddles for classmates.

quests.title: Last Watched
quests.text: Ask a classmate: 'What was the last film or series you watched? Did you like it?' Write 3 sentences about the answer. Useful phrases: 'He/She watched ...', 'It was ...', 'He/She liked / didn't like it because ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Look for past simple forms (watched, was, liked) and third-person reporting.

quests.title: Weekend Fun
quests.text: Ask 3 classmates: 'What are you going to watch, play or listen to this weekend?' Write 3 sentences. Useful phrases: '... is going to ...', 'I'm going to ...', 'We both like ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Practises 'going to' for plans. Students with no plans can invent one.

quests.title: Star Rating
quests.text: Tell 4 classmates about a song you love. Ask: 'Do you know it? Give it 1 to 5 stars.' Write 3 sentences: 'I asked ... people. Most people gave ... stars. One person said ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Students may need to describe the song if nobody knows it. Check numbers and 'most people'.

quests.title: Guess The Hero
quests.text: Choose a character from a game, film or cartoon. Describe it to a classmate, but do not say the name. Use: 'It has ...', 'It is ...', 'It can ...'. Your classmate guesses. Write 3 sentences: who you chose and if the guess was right.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage describing personality and abilities, not just colour. Good for a quick guessing game.

quests.title: Book Or Film
quests.text: Ask a classmate: 'Which is better, the book or the film of the same story?' Choose a story you both know, or any story you like. Give reasons and ask follow-up questions. Useful phrases: 'In my opinion ...', 'I agree because ...', 'I see your point, but ...'. Write 3-5 sentences about your views.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives and reasons. If they have not read a book, they can compare a film and a game or series.

quests.title: Playlist Deal
quests.text: Make a playlist of 4 songs with 2 or 3 classmates. Everyone suggests one song and says why it is good. Then choose the 4 best songs together. Keep the songs suitable for school. Useful phrases: 'How about ...?', 'I'd rather ...', 'That's a good idea, but ...'. Write 3-5 sentences: the songs and why you chose them.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for polite negotiation language. Students should explain choices rather than just list titles.

quests.title: Quick Review
quests.text: Write a short review of a film, series or game you know well. Give it a score out of 10 and say one good point and one bad point. Send it to a classmate and ask: 'Do you agree?' Useful phrases: 'I'd give it ... out of 10', 'The best part is ...', 'It could be better if ...'. Write your review in 3-5 sentences.
quests.teacherNote: Check the balance of positive and negative points and use of 'could be better if'. Avoid spoilers.

quests.title: Rules Explained
quests.text: Explain the rules of a game you know (video game, board game or sport) to a classmate in the chat. Your classmate asks 3 questions to check. Then swap roles. Useful phrases: 'First, you ...', 'If you ..., you ...', 'Do you mean ...?'. Write 3-5 sentences about the game your partner explained.
quests.teacherNote: Look for sequencers (first, then, after that), simple conditionals and real clarifying questions. Any game is fine, including sports or card games.

quests.title: Surprising Favourite
quests.text: Tell 2 classmates about a song, film or game you love that people may not expect. Ask them to guess why you like it, then explain. Listen to their favourites too. Useful phrases: 'I bet you like it because ...', 'Actually, ...', 'That's surprising because ...'. Write 3-5 sentences.
quests.teacherNote: Keep the tone kind: no one should laugh at another person's taste. Look for speculation language such as 'I bet' and 'maybe'.

quests.title: Movie Afternoon Pitch
quests.text: Your class can watch one film together. With 2 or 3 classmates, each person pitches a different film in 2 or 3 sentences, using reasons that will appeal to everyone. Then discuss objections and vote for one film that is suitable for the whole class. Write a short paragraph: the film you chose, the strongest argument for it, and one objection you answered.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive language and answers to objections. Films should be age-appropriate; steer students away from anything unsuitable.

quests.title: Games Debate Swap
quests.text: Discuss with 3 classmates: 'Video games are a waste of time.' First, each person argues for or against, even if it is not their real opinion. Then swap sides. Finally, summarise the strongest points on each side and say what you really think. Useful phrases: 'On the one hand ...', 'That said, ...', 'It depends on ...'. Write a short paragraph with a balanced summary and your conclusion.
quests.teacherNote: The side swap forces students to understand opposing views. Check for contrast connectors and a clear personal conclusion.

quests.title: Sequel Or Original
quests.text: With a classmate, discuss this idea: 'Original stories are always better than sequels and remakes.' Give examples from films, series or games you both know. Imagine a studio asked you for advice. Agree on three rules for making a good sequel. Write a short paragraph with your three rules and the reasons for them.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for would/should and examples. A good outcome shows reasons for each rule and a real compromise between partners.

quests.title: My Week The Series
quests.text: Imagine that your school week were a TV series. Ask 2 or 3 classmates what genre it would be, which song would be its theme tune, and what the title of this week's episode would be. Explain your own answers with reasons, and ask each person why they chose theirs. Write a short paragraph describing the series that suits your group best.
quests.teacherNote: Keep the humour kind and about situations, not people. Look for 'would' and justified creative choices.

quests.title: Game Design Meeting
quests.text: Design a new video game with 3 classmates. Agree on the genre, the hero, the main goal and one rule that makes your game different. Everyone must suggest ideas, and you must compromise when you disagree. Then write a short paragraph pitching your game to a publisher. Explain who would enjoy it and why it would be a success.
quests.teacherNote: Look for compromise language and persuasive pitching. Games should be non-violent or suitable for school; adapt as needed.

quests.title: Dream Job Hunt
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates in nearby chat: "What is your dream job?" Answer their question too. Then write 2 sentences: "My dream job is ... ." and "(name) wants to be ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Check a/an with jobs (a vet, an astronaut) and the -s in "wants". For an extra challenge, ask students to find someone with the same dream job as them.

quests.title: Dream Holiday Pick
quests.text: Message a classmate: "Do you want to go to the beach, the mountains or a city?" Say your choice. Write: "I want to ... because ... . My partner wants to ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Look for "wants" with -s for the partner and a simple reason after "because". Fast pairs can invent a fourth place (a desert island, the Moon) and ask another classmate.

quests.title: Space Job Scramble
quests.text: Put the letters in order to find a dream job: T-U-A-N-O-R-T-S-A. Clue: this person works in space. Ask a classmate: "Do you want this job?" Type the job.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: ASTRONAUT (the 9 letters T-U-A-N-O-R-T-S-A make only this word). Fast finishers can make a scrambled job for a classmate to solve in the chat.

quests.title: Dream Island Team
quests.text: Imagine a dream island with 2 or 3 classmates. Each person says one thing on it in nearby chat: "There is a ... ." Then write: "Our dream island has ... and ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Check "there is a" with singular nouns and "has". Fast groups can add a name for the island and post it in the chat so the class can vote for a favourite.

quests.title: Fountain Wishes
quests.text: Go to the fountain with a classmate. Each of you makes a wish in nearby chat: "I wish for ... ." Then write: "My wish is ... . My partner wishes for ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Encourage fun, imaginative wishes (a pet dragon, a pizza tree) rather than personal ones. Check "wishes" with -es for the partner.

quests.title: Weekend Plans Match
quests.text: Ask classmates in nearby chat: "What are you going to do this weekend?" Find 2 people with a plan like yours (or a plan you like). Useful phrases: "I'm going to ...", "Me too!", "Really? That sounds fun!" Write 3 sentences about your plan and the 2 people you found.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for "I'm going to + verb" and the correct question form. Remind students that "relax at home" is a perfectly good plan, so nobody feels left out.

quests.title: Pixel Plaza 2050
quests.text: Imagine Pixel Plaza in the year 2050 with 2 or 3 classmates. Decide together what is going to be different at the hotel, the cafe and the park. Useful phrases: "The cafe is going to have ...", "There are going to be ...". Write 3 sentences, one for each place.
quests.teacherNote: Check "there are going to be" + plural nouns. Groups can walk to each place and post their idea there in nearby chat.

quests.title: Bolt's Big Birthday
quests.text: Read: "Bolt the robot was built on 5 May 2026. On 5 May 2050, Bolt is going to have a big party." How old is Bolt going to be at the party? Check your answer with a classmate. Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 24 (2050 minus 2026; the party is on the exact date Bolt was built, so there is no 23/24 doubt). Fast finishers can write their own robot birthday puzzle for a classmate in the chat.

quests.title: Last Year, Next Year
quests.text: Message a classmate. Ask: "What new thing did you learn last year?" and "What new thing are you going to try next year?" Ask "Why?" too. Then answer their questions. Useful phrases: "Last year I learned to ...", "Next year I'm going to try ...". Write 3 sentences about your partner.
quests.teacherNote: Look for correct past forms (learned/learnt, did you learn) and "going to + verb"; partners should report in third person ("She learned to ...").

quests.title: Fortune Cafe
quests.text: Go to the cafe and be a fortune teller! Give 4 classmates a kind, funny prediction in nearby chat: "Next week you are going to ...". Keep it kind. Ask for a prediction too. Write 3 sentences: two predictions you gave and your favourite one you got.
quests.teacherNote: Predictions must be kind and silly ("you are going to find a lost sock"), never about looks or anything personal; moderate the chat for unkind messages. Check "you are going to + verb".

quests.title: Moon Base or Sea Base
quests.text: Ask at least 4 classmates in nearby chat: "In 2050, would you rather live in a city on the Moon or under the sea?" Ask a follow-up question each time, like "What would you miss most?" Keep count of the answers. Useful phrases: "I'd rather ... because ...", "That's a good point, but ...". Write 4 sentences: the results, the most interesting reason you heard, and your own choice with a reason.
quests.teacherNote: Check "I'd rather + base verb" (not "I'd rather to live"). Results can be given as "3 out of 5 people ...", a good chance to practise comparisons.

quests.title: Dream Job Detective
quests.text: Solve this puzzle. Mia, Leo and Sara each want a different dream job: chef, pilot or vet. Leo is afraid of flying. Sara is allergic to cats and dogs. Mia wants to work with animals. Who wants to be the pilot? Explain your thinking to a classmate in nearby chat before you answer. Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "So ... must be the ...". Type only the name.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Sara. Mia works with animals, so she is the vet; Leo is afraid of flying, so he can't be the pilot and must be the chef; that leaves Sara as the pilot. Sara's allergy is an extra clue that she can't be the vet.

quests.title: Time Capsule Team
quests.text: Plan a time capsule for Pixel Plaza players in 2050 with 2 or 3 classmates. Each person suggests one object and explains why it shows life today. Discuss and agree on the best three. Useful phrases: "We should include ... because ...", "I think ... is more important than ...", "OK, let's choose ...". Write 4 sentences: the three objects your group chose and why, and one idea you didn't choose.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for suggestions and comparatives (more important than, better than). The objects are imaginary, so no real items are needed; a follow-up question could be "What will students in 2050 think of it?"

quests.title: Future Me Interview
quests.text: Interview a classmate by direct message about their life at age 25. Ask at least 4 questions with "will", for example "What job will you have?" or "Will you have a pet?" After each answer, ask a follow-up question. Then swap roles. Useful phrases: "I think I'll ...", "I probably won't ...", "Maybe I'll ...". Write 4 sentences about your partner's future life.
quests.teacherNote: Check "will + base verb" and adverb position ("I'll probably ...", "I probably won't ..."). Students should report in third person ("She thinks she'll be a vet") and keep to fun topics, not where people will live exactly.

quests.title: The If Chain
quests.text: Build an "if chain" in nearby chat with 2 or 3 classmates. Start: "If I find a time machine, I will visit the dinosaurs." The next person begins with the end of that sentence: "If I visit the dinosaurs, I will ..." Keep going for at least 8 sentences. Useful phrases: "If I ..., I will ...", "If that happens, ...". Write your 4 favourite sentences from the chain, in order.
quests.teacherNote: Check the first conditional pattern (if + present simple, will + verb); the typical error is "If I will go". The chain can be as silly as students like as long as it stays kind.

quests.title: Invention Prize Jury
quests.text: Hold the Pixel Plaza Invention Prize with 2 or 3 classmates. Each person pitches an invention that would make life in the future easier or more fun. After each pitch, the others ask tough questions, such as "What would happen if it broke?" or "Who would actually use it?" Then negotiate a winner; nobody can vote for their own idea. Useful phrases: "Imagine if ...", "The main advantage is ...", "I see your point, but ...". Write a short paragraph: summarise the inventions, explain which one won and why, and mention one doubt your group still has about it.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive language and hypotheticals (it would save time, if it broke we could ...). To adapt, give each group a theme such as school, sport or the environment.

quests.title: Superpower Swap Meet
quests.text: Choose a starting superpower: reading minds, teleporting, talking to animals or stopping time. Then mingle in nearby chat and try to swap it for a better one. To get a swap, convince classmates that your power is more useful than theirs, but be honest about one downside if they ask. Make at least 3 offers. Useful phrases: "If you had my power, you could ...", "I'd swap, but only if ...", "Think about it: ...". Write a short paragraph: which power you started and finished with, which arguments worked best and why you think so.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for the second conditional (if you had ..., you could ...) and conditions (only if, as long as). The downsides students mention (e.g. hearing everyone's thoughts) make a good whole-class debrief.

quests.title: Robots at Work Debate
quests.text: Debate this statement in a group of 3 or 4: "In the future, robots will do most jobs, and that is a good thing." Split into two sides, even if you disagree with yours. After a few minutes, switch sides. Finally, drop your roles and try to find a view everyone can accept. Useful phrases: "On the one hand ...", "That might be true, but ...", "What worries me is ...". Write a short paragraph summarising the strongest argument on each side and your own honest opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Check that summaries represent both sides fairly and use hedging (might, could, probably). With a group of 3, one side is a single person, or the third student acts as a judge who summarises both sides.

quests.title: Message from 2050
quests.text: Imagine you travel back from the year 2050 and can give today's teenagers three pieces of advice. Choose them and think how you would justify each one. Tell your best advice to a classmate in nearby chat and ask whether they would follow it and why. Then listen to theirs. Useful phrases: "If I were you, I'd ...", "By 2050, you will have ...", "You might regret it if ...". Write a short paragraph: your three pieces of advice, your reasons, and how your classmate reacted.
quests.teacherNote: Look for advice structures (If I were you, you should, you might regret) and the future perfect (will have + past participle). Fun advice about technology, school or the planet works well; steer away from personal topics.

quests.title: The Frog's Wish
focus: Conditions: as long as / only if
quests.text: Meet a classmate on the little bridge in the park. A magic frog from the pond offers you one shared wish, but every wish comes with a catch. Take turns: one of you proposes a wish, the other invents a funny catch, for example "You can fly, but only at walking speed." Negotiate, changing the wording each time, until you find a wish you would both accept. Useful phrases: "That's fine as long as ...", "What if we changed it to ...?", "I'd only agree if ...". Write a short paragraph: your best rejected wish, your final wish and how you agreed.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for conditions (as long as, provided that, only if) and suggestions with "what if we ...". The catches should stay funny, not scary or mean.

quests.title: Where To Next?
quests.text: Ask four classmates in the chat: "Where do you want to go on holiday?" Then ask "Why?" Write 2 sentences: "... wants to go to ... because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Listen for the third-person -s in "wants" and simple because-clauses. For a challenge, ask students to find two classmates with the same dream place.

quests.title: Odd One Out
quests.text: Find the word that is not a country: Italy, Japan, Paris, Brazil, Canada. Write the answer: "... is not a country." Then send a new puzzle like this to a classmate.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Paris, because it is a city and the other four are countries. Answers like "Paris is not a country" are accepted; the whispered puzzles are a nice extra to read in the chat.

quests.title: ABC Suitcase
quests.text: Pack an ABC suitcase with a partner. Take turns: "I pack an apple." "I pack a book." "I pack a cap." How far can you go? Write your last 3 things: "We pack ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check a/an (an apple, an umbrella, a map). Tricky letters like Q, X and Z can be skipped, or students can invent funny items.

quests.title: World Cafe Menu
quests.text: Go to the cafe with 2 or 3 classmates. Each person names a food and its country: "Sushi is from Japan." Find 4 different foods. Write 2 sentences: "... is from ..."
quests.teacherNote: Expect pizza, pasta and sushi; praise less obvious ones (curry from India, crepes from France). If the chat blocks a dish name, students can describe it in English, e.g. "a rice dish from Spain".

quests.title: Where Am I?
quests.text: Play a guessing game with a partner. Think of a country. Give two clues: "It is hot. I see kangaroos." Your partner guesses. Swap. Write 2 sentences: "My partner's country is ... One clue is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Good clues mention weather, animals, food or famous places. If guessing takes too long, allow a third clue.

quests.title: Holiday Memory Hunt
quests.text: Find a different classmate for each one: saw snow, swam in the sea, ate food from another country, visited a museum. Ask: "Did you see snow last year?" Useful phrases: "Yes, I did." "No, I didn't." Write 3 sentences: "... saw snow last year."
quests.teacherNote: Look for "Did you + base verb" in the questions and past forms (saw, swam, ate) in the journal. The items are everyday ones so nobody is left out; in small classes one classmate can cover two items.

quests.title: Pixel Hotel Check-In
quests.text: Meet a partner at the hotel. One person is the receptionist and one is a tourist with a funny pretend name. Useful phrases: "How many nights?" "Do you want breakfast?" "Here is your key." Then swap. Write 3 sentences about your tourist, for example: "Captain Pizza wants a room for 4 nights."
quests.teacherNote: Pretend names keep real personal data out; make sure nobody uses a classmate's name as a joke. Stronger pairs can add a problem, like no rooms with a view of the pond.

quests.title: Travel Riddle Time
quests.text: Solve this riddle with a partner. I am a small book. I have your photo and your name. You show me at the airport when you travel to another country. What am I? Useful phrases: "I think it is ...", "Maybe it is ...". Type the answer. Then send your own travel riddle to your partner.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: a passport (a small book with a photo and name, shown at the border). The extra step, whispering an own riddle, lets students practise "It is ... You use it to ...".

quests.title: Postcard From Paradise
quests.text: Choose a dream holiday place with 2 or 3 classmates. Make a group postcard from there: take turns adding one sentence in the chat. Useful phrases: "Yesterday we visited ...", "We ate ...", "The weather was ...". Write your 3 favourite sentences in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple forms (visited, ate, saw, went). For extra fun, add a rule that every sentence must include one silly surprise.

quests.title: Lost Tourist Rescue
quests.text: Play "Lost Tourist" with a partner. The tourist starts at the hotel and asks: "Excuse me, how do I get to the bridge?" The guide sends directions. Useful phrases: "Go past the fountain", "Turn left at the cafe". The tourist walks there. Then swap. Write your best directions in 2 or 3 sentences.
quests.teacherNote: On a top-down map, pairs may need to agree that left and right mean the screen's left and right. When they swap, the new tourist chooses a different place, such as the shop or the pond.

quests.title: The Travel Agent Game
quests.text: Work with a partner: one is a travel agent and one is a customer. The agent asks at least 5 questions (hot or cold? city or nature? favourite food?) and follow-up questions like "Why?" Then the agent recommends a destination and explains why it is perfect. Swap roles. Useful phrases: "What kind of ... do you prefer?", "I'd recommend ... because ...". Write 4 sentences: what your customer likes, where you sent them and why.
quests.teacherNote: Good answers link the customer's likes to the destination (loves snow and wildlife, so Canada or Norway). To stretch strong pairs, the customer can reject the first idea and ask for another.

quests.title: Four Tickets Puzzle
quests.text: Solve this puzzle with a classmate. Four friends have tickets to Tokyo, Cairo, Rome and Rio de Janeiro, one city each. Ben wants to see the pyramids. Ana is not going to Asia or South America. Dani wants to dance at a famous carnival near the beach. Where is Carla going? Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "So ... must be going to ...". Write the city.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Tokyo. Ben goes to Cairo (the famous pyramids are in Egypt) and Dani to Rio (carnival), so Ana, who is not going to Asia, gets Rome and Carla gets Tokyo.

quests.title: The Perfect Travel Buddy
quests.text: Find out what makes a perfect travel buddy. Ask at least 4 classmates: "Which is most important in a travel buddy: being funny, being organised or liking the same food?" Always ask a follow-up question, like "Why?" or "Can you give an example?" Useful phrases: "For me, the most important thing is ...", "I'd rather travel with someone who ...". Write 4 sentences: the most popular answer, one interesting reason, and your own opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage real follow-up questions rather than just collecting votes. Change the three qualities (brave, calm, good with maps) to make a second round feel fresh.

quests.title: Travel Truth Or Lie
quests.text: Play a travel version of Two Truths and a Lie with 2 or 3 classmates. Tell three statements about trips: two true and one invented, for example: "Last summer I missed a train in Italy." Your classmates ask follow-up questions, then guess the lie. Useful phrases: "Where were you when ...?", "What happened next?", "I think number two is the lie because ...". Write 4 sentences: the best story you heard, what you asked and what you guessed.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for past simple and past continuous in the stories and for real follow-up questions. Students may invent all three statements, so nobody has to share private experiences.

quests.title: Travel Would You Rather
quests.text: Play "Would you rather" with 2 or 3 classmates. Take turns asking travel questions, for example: "Would you rather travel by train for two days or fly for twelve hours?" or "Would you rather visit a jungle or a desert?" Everyone answers and gives a reason. Useful phrases: "I'd rather ... because ...", "That's true, but ...". Write 4 sentences: your favourite question, what people chose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Students should invent their own questions after the two examples. Check "I'd rather + base verb" (not "I'd rather to").

quests.title: The Class Trip Showdown
quests.text: Imagine your class has won a free trip, but your group must choose the destination: a city break in London, a nature trip to Iceland, or five days at a theme park. Share out the options so each one has a defender, then persuade each other. Ask tough questions, point out weaknesses and negotiate until everyone accepts one choice or a clever compromise. Useful phrases: "Imagine how amazing it would be if ...", "I see your point, but ...", "What if we ...?" Write a short paragraph summarising the arguments for each option and how your group reached its final decision.
quests.teacherNote: Look for concession language (I see your point, but...; that may be true, however...). You can swap the three options for places your class is studying.

quests.title: The Backpack Dilemma
quests.text: Imagine you and a partner are backpacking around the world for a month and your bags are almost full. Between you, you can add only three more items (no phones or money). Each of you proposes three items and explains why they are essential. Then negotiate until you agree on a final three. Useful phrases: "Without a ..., we'd be in trouble if ...", "I could live without ... as long as ...", "Fair enough, but ...". Write a short paragraph explaining your final three items, what you gave up and why.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for conditionals (we'd be in trouble if it rained) and concession language. Reward creative items, like a deck of cards or a sewing kit, when the reasons are convincing.

quests.title: The Great Tourism Debate
quests.text: Interview at least 4 classmates about tourism in popular cities like Barcelona or Venice: "Is tourism good or bad for a busy city?" Use follow-ups like "Who benefits most?" or "What would you change if you were the mayor?" Try to find different points of view, and keep it respectful: talk about tourism, not nationalities. Useful phrases: "On the one hand ..., on the other hand ...", "It depends on ...", "Most people think ..., whereas ...". Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and giving your own balanced opinion.
quests.teacherNote: This topic is close to home in Catalonia, so steer students away from generalisations about nationalities and party politics. Strong paragraphs balance benefits (jobs, culture) and problems (crowds, noise, prices) before giving an opinion.

quests.title: Time Machine Tours
quests.text: Imagine you run a time-travel tour company. Invent one holiday to any city, past or future: ancient Rome, London in the 1960s, Tokyo in the year 3000. Go to the square and pitch your tour to at least 4 classmates: what they would see, eat and do, and why it is worth the risk. Listen to their pitches and ask tricky questions. Useful phrases: "If you came with us, you would ...", "Don't worry about ..., because ...", "I'd be tempted, but ...". Write a short paragraph: how many people you persuaded, the best pitch you heard and which tour you would choose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Keep destinations light-hearted and steer away from wars or disasters. Listen for second conditionals (If you came with us, you would...) and persuasive questions.

quests.title: Pixel Plaza Guidebook
quests.text: Write a guidebook entry about Pixel Plaza for visitors. Include a must-see place, a hidden gem and one honest warning. Use relative clauses ("the cafe, which ...") and phrases like "is famous for". Show your draft to two classmates, ask what they would add or change, and improve it. Useful phrases: "... is well worth a visit, whereas ...", "Visitors tend to ...", "Don't miss ...". Write your final entry as a short paragraph.
quests.teacherNote: Look for relative clauses, balanced description (praise plus an honest warning) and real use of classmates' feedback. A nice follow-up is to read two or three entries aloud and compare them.

quests.title: Cafe Menu Mash-Up
quests.text: Ask a classmate: "What is your favourite food?" Make a new cafe dish with their food and your favourite food. Tell them! Write 1 sentence: "New at the cafe: ... with ...!"
quests.teacherNote: Expect funny mixes like "pizza with chocolate"; check food words and the preposition "with". Fast finishers can invent a name for the dish.

quests.title: Colour Poem Crew
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "What is your favourite colour?" Find a thing in Pixel Plaza for each colour. Write a 3-line poem and share it: "Red is the ... Blue is the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Accept anything students can see in the town (the pond, a hat, the cafe door). If a colour is hard to find, let them use any thing they know in that colour.

quests.title: Shop Slogan Shout
quests.text: Write a slogan for the shop: "Come to the shop! We have ... and ...!" Say it in nearby chat. Ask a classmate: "Do you like it?" Write your slogan and their answer.
quests.teacherNote: Check "We have" + plural nouns (hats, apples). Stronger students can add an adjective: "We have cool hats and big apples!"

quests.title: Postcard from the Pond
quests.text: Go to the park. Write a postcard to a classmate and send it: "Hi ...! I am in the park. I can see ... and ...!" Ask them to write back. Write your postcard.
quests.teacherNote: Students walk to the park first, so check they name things that are really there (the pond, the bridge, classmates' avatars). Partners can compare postcards afterwards.

quests.title: Birthday Card for the Fountain
quests.text: Make a birthday card for the fountain! Ask four classmates for a nice word, like "happy" or "sunny". Write your card: "Happy birthday, Fountain! Have a ..., ..., ... and ... day!"
quests.teacherNote: Check that students collect adjectives (not nouns) and use commas in the list. The card is for the fountain, not a real student, so nobody has to share their real birthday.

quests.title: The Duck's Diary
quests.text: Imagine you are a duck in the park pond. With a partner, write the duck's diary about yesterday. Take turns in direct messages: you write one sentence, your partner writes the next. Useful phrases: "Dear Diary, yesterday I...", "Then I saw...", "In the evening...". Write your diary (3 sentences).
quests.teacherNote: Check irregular past forms (swam, ate, saw, flew) and sequencing words. Pairs can read their diary in nearby chat at the pond.

quests.title: Lost: One Magic Hat
quests.text: Write a "Lost!" poster for your magic hat. Say what it looks like, what it can do and where you lost it. Useful phrases: "It is ...", "It can ...", "I lost it near the ...". Post it in nearby chat and ask four classmates: "Did you see it?" Write your poster (3 sentences).
quests.teacherNote: Look for adjective order (a big purple hat) and "can" for abilities. Encourage classmates to reply with funny sightings ("I saw it at the cafe!").

quests.title: The Weekend Song
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "What are you going to do this weekend?" Real or silly answers are fine! Use them to write a song chorus. Useful phrases: "On Saturday, ... is going to ...", "We're going to have fun!" Post it in nearby chat. Write your chorus (3 lines).
quests.teacherNote: Check "is/are going to" + base verb. Give a bonus for rhymes (play/day, fun/sun). Remind students that silly answers are welcome so nobody has to share private plans.

quests.title: Soup Surprise
quests.text: Meet two classmates at the cafe and choose roles: customer, waiter and cook. Write a funny dialogue in nearby chat: something strange is in the soup! Useful phrases: "Excuse me, there's a ... in my soup!", "I'm so sorry!", "It's today's special!" Write your dialogue (at least 3 lines).
quests.teacherNote: Encourage silly objects (a tiny dinosaur, a sock) and polite phrases. Groups can perform their dialogue for the class at the cafe.

quests.title: Tongue Twister Trouble
