quests.text: Choose a letter with a partner. Together, write a funny tongue twister where most words start with that letter, like "Six silly snakes sell socks." Send it to another classmate: "Can you type this fast?" Write your tongue twister and what happened.
quests.teacherNote: Check that the tongue twister is a real sentence (subject + verb + object). Later, ask volunteers to say theirs aloud in class for real pronunciation practice.

quests.title: Pixel Plaza Anthem
quests.text: Write a song for Pixel Plaza with two or three classmates. Each person chooses a favourite place in town and explains why in the chat. Turn the reasons into a 4-line chorus, then agree on the best order and a title. Useful phrases: "My favourite place is ... because ...", "What about putting ... first?", "I think this line sounds better because ..." Write your chorus with its title and one sentence explaining why you chose that order.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for reasons with "because" and polite agreeing and disagreeing while they order the lines. For a bonus, ask the group to make two lines rhyme.

quests.title: Mystery Box Story Chain
quests.text: Start a story in nearby chat at the cafe: "One morning, a mysterious box appeared on a table, and..." Ask at least four classmates to add one sentence each, and keep it going with follow-up questions like "What was inside?" or "What happened next?" Useful phrases: "Can you add the next part?", "I love your idea because..." Write the story in 4 sentences (shorten it if needed), then one more sentence: which idea did you like most, and why?
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple and linking words (then, suddenly, after that). If the cafe gets crowded, start a second chain at the hotel or the pond.

quests.title: Time Capsule Letter
quests.text: Write a letter with a partner for a time capsule that students will open in 2050. First, discuss: what is Pixel Plaza like today, and how will it be different? Compare your ideas. Useful phrases: "Today the cafe is ..., but in 2050 it will be ...", "I think the hotel will be bigger than ...", "Do you agree?" Write your letter in 4-5 sentences, starting "Dear students of 2050,".
quests.teacherNote: Look for "will" + comparatives (bigger, more modern, quieter). Pairs can whisper their letter to another pair and compare predictions.

quests.title: Haiku by the Bridge
quests.text: Go to the little bridge in the park and write a haiku about what you see: three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables, for example "Calm water below" (5). Use / between lines. Send it to two classmates and ask for their opinion, then improve one line. Useful phrases: "Which line do you like best, and why?", "Would you change anything?" Write your final haiku and two sentences about your classmates' feedback.
quests.teacherNote: Do not be strict about syllables; reward vivid words and clear feedback sentences ("She liked line 2 because..."). Show a model haiku first if the class has never seen one.

quests.title: Superhero of the Park
quests.text: Create a superhero who protects the park, together with two or three classmates. Each person suggests a name, a power and a funny weakness; then vote on the best ideas and give reasons. Useful phrases: "I prefer ... because ...", "Flying is cooler than ...", "Let's go with ..." Write a hero profile in 4-5 sentences: name, power, weakness, and how the hero saved the park last week.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for suggestions and reasons during the vote, and past simple in the rescue story. Groups can introduce their hero to the class at the fountain.

quests.title: Fairy Tale Remix (Creative Writing with Classmates)
quests.text: Remix a famous fairy tale with two or three classmates: choose one everyone knows, such as Cinderella or Little Red Riding Hood, and give it a modern twist. Each person proposes how the story should change and defends the idea; negotiate a plot that everyone can accept, even if it means compromising. Useful phrases: "Wouldn't it be funnier if...?", "I'd be willing to drop that if...", "Suppose the hero were..." Write a short paragraph: the original tale, your twist, and which idea you gave up and why.
quests.teacherNote: Assess the negotiating and compromise language, not just the story. Groups can share their twist in nearby chat and the class can vote for the funniest remix.

quests.title: Proverbs for Pixel Plaza
quests.text: Invent two new proverbs with a partner, like "A bridge is only as strong as the friends who cross it." Each proverb must teach a lesson about friendship, teamwork or town life. Then ask two classmates what each proverb means and whether they agree with its advice; explain what you meant if they misunderstand. Useful phrases: "To my mind it suggests...", "That's not quite what we meant; we wanted to say...", "It could also be read as...", "If someone followed this advice, they would..." Write a short paragraph: your proverbs, how classmates interpreted them, and which one worked best.
quests.teacherNote: Look for speculation (it could mean...) and conditionals when students explain the advice. Ask for the best proverb to be shared with the whole class.

quests.title: If the Fountain Could Talk
quests.text: Give the fountain in the square a voice! Write a short monologue as the fountain: what it has seen, what it would do if it could move, and what it would ask the people walking past. Share it in nearby chat at the fountain and ask a classmate: "How would you react if the fountain really talked?" Useful phrases: "If I could ..., I would ...", "I've seen so many ...", "If it spoke to me, I'd ..." Write a short paragraph: your monologue plus a summary of your classmate's reaction.
quests.teacherNote: Check the second conditional (If I could..., I would...) and present perfect for experiences (I've seen...). Stronger students can add a reply from the pond or the bridge.

quests.title: Pixel Plaza: The Movie
quests.text: Write the trailer for a movie set in Pixel Plaza! First, mingle with at least four classmates and ask: "What kind of film should it be (comedy, adventure, mystery...)?" "Who or what would the hero be?" "What would go wrong?" Useful phrases: "Most people wanted..., although a few...", "If it were a comedy, the hero would..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views, then your trailer voice-over, starting "In a town where..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for reporting language (most people, a few, while others) and a clear summary before the trailer. Volunteers can perform their trailer in nearby chat in the square.

quests.title: Shop of Impossible Things
quests.text: Open the Shop of Impossible Things with a partner: invent a product that cannot exist, like bottled sunshine or a jar of silence. Write a persuasive advert together, then persuade another classmate to try it and invite them to ask tough questions. Answer their doubts until they decide. Useful phrases: "Imagine never having to... again!", "If you tried it, you'd...", "I understand your concern, but..." Write a short paragraph: your advert, the customer's main doubt, and whether you convinced them.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive structures and how students answer objections politely. Finish with a class vote for the most convincing impossible product.

quests.title: Meet Me There
quests.text: Pick a place, like the cafe. Message a partner: "Meet me at the ...!" Walk there and say hello. Write: "I meet ... at the ... and we say hello."
quests.teacherNote: Check the use of "at the" + place and simple greetings. For a quick extension, the partner chooses the next meeting place and they play again.

quests.title: Letter Jumble
quests.text: Put the letters in order to find a place in the Plaza: NUOTAFNI. Ask a classmate: "Is it the ...?" Walk there and type the place.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: fountain (NUOTAFNI is FOUNTAIN with the letters mixed up). Fast finishers can mix up another place name, like PARK or HOTEL, and whisper it to a classmate to solve.

quests.title: Where Are You?
quests.text: Send "Where are you?" to four classmates. They answer: "I am at/near the ...". Write about two of them: "... is at the ... and ... is near the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Listen for "at the" vs "near the". Stronger students can try "between the ... and the ..." or "next to the ...".

quests.title: Look and Tell
quests.text: Go to the fountain or the pond. Look around. Ask a classmate: "What can you see?" Tell them what you see too. Write: "At the ..., I can see ... and ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answers depend on what each student really sees, so any honest description is correct. Encourage friendly replies in the chat like "I can see ... too!".

quests.title: My Top Spot
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "What is your favourite place in the Plaza?" Tell them your favourite too. Write: "My favourite place is the ... because it is ..." Add one sentence about a classmate.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage simple adjectives after "it is" (quiet, big, pretty, fun). A good classmate sentence is "... likes the ... because it is ...".

quests.title: Lost Tourist
quests.text: Start at the hotel with a partner. You are a lost tourist. Ask: "Excuse me, how do I get to the park?" Your partner gives directions and you follow them. Then swap roles. Useful phrases: go straight on, turn left, turn right, next to. Write 3 sentences about the directions you got.
quests.teacherNote: Check that directions use imperatives and place phrases (next to, in front of, between). After the swap, the new tourist can ask for the cafe, the shop or the bridge.

quests.title: Plaza Hide and Seek
quests.text: Choose a secret place in the Plaza and go there. Send three clues to two or three classmates, but don't say the name! Useful phrases: "It's near the...", "You can ... there", "It has...". When they find you, say "Well done!" Write 3 sentences: your place, your clues and who found you.
quests.teacherNote: Good clues describe without naming the place (e.g. "You can drink hot chocolate there"). If seekers get stuck, the hider can give one extra clue with a direction.

quests.title: Next Stop Survey
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "Where are you going to go next?" and "What are you going to do there?" Tell them your plan too. Useful phrases: I'm going to walk to..., I'm going to meet... Write 3 sentences about their plans, like: "... is going to go to the ... to ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check "going to + verb" and "to + verb" for purpose (to buy a drink, to see the pond). As a follow-up, students can walk to a place a classmate mentioned and meet them there.

quests.title: Water Under My Feet
quests.text: Read this message from a friend: "I'm in the park. There is water under my feet, but I'm not wet!" Where is your friend? Check with a classmate: "Do you think it's the ...?" Walk there, then type the place.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: bridge (the little bridge in the park is the only place where you stand above water and stay dry). Fast finishers can write a similar message about another place and whisper it to a classmate.

quests.title: Tiny Tour Guide
quests.text: Be a tour guide! Take two or three classmates to three places in the Plaza. At each place, tell them one thing about it, like "This is the cafe. You can..." After the tour, write 3 sentences in the past simple: "First we went to... Then we... Finally..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for sequencing words (first, then, after that, finally) and past forms (went, saw, walked). To make it more interactive, the tourists ask the guide one question at each stop.

quests.title: Friday Meeting Spot
quests.text: Work with two or three classmates. Imagine you want to meet in the Plaza every Friday after school. Each person suggests a place and gives a reason. Compare the places and agree on one. Useful phrases: "I think the ... is better because...", "That's a good idea, but...", "What about the ...?" Then walk there together. Write 4 sentences: the places you compared, the place you chose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for comparatives with reasons (quieter, closer, more fun) and polite disagreement. If the group cannot agree, they can vote and explain the result.

quests.title: Mystery Route
quests.text: Choose a secret destination, but don't tell your partner. Start together at the fountain. Send directions one step at a time; your partner follows them without knowing where they are going. Then swap. Useful phrases: "Walk past the...", "Keep going until you reach...", "It's on your left." Write 4 sentences: your directions, where your partner arrived, and which instruction was the most useful or the most confusing and why.
quests.teacherNote: Good directions use landmarks (past the cafe, until you reach the bridge) rather than only left/right, which depends on the way an avatar is facing. Ask pairs to share their most confusing instruction and improve it together.

quests.title: Live From the Plaza
quests.text: Be a TV reporter! Go to the square or the park and report what is happening right now. Describe what avatars are doing and wearing, and ask one person nearby: "What are you doing here today?" Useful phrases: "Right now, someone in a ... hat is...", "People are...", "It looks like..." Write a 4-sentence news report in the present continuous and add your opinion: is it a good place to be today, and why?
quests.teacherNote: Check present continuous forms (is walking, are chatting). Remind students to describe avatars kindly (hats, shirts, colours) and never comment on real people.

quests.title: Square vs Park
quests.text: Work with a partner. One of you goes to the square and the other goes to the park. Send each other direct messages about three things you can see. Then compare: which place is busier, quieter or more colourful? Ask a follow-up question, like "What is the best thing there?" Useful phrases: "The park is busier than...", "Both places have...", "The square has..., but the park..." Write 4 sentences comparing the two places.
quests.teacherNote: Answers depend on what students see on the day, so any honest comparison is fine. Check comparative forms (busier, more colourful) and linkers like but, both and whereas.

quests.title: Plaza Find Someone Who
quests.text: Find a different classmate for each: someone who has walked over the bridge today, someone who prefers the cafe to the shop, someone who thinks the park is the best place, and someone who can explain the way from the hotel to the pond. Ask one follow-up question each time. Useful phrases: "Have you ... today?", "Do you prefer ... or ...?", "Can you tell me how to...?" Write 4 sentences about what you found out.
quests.teacherNote: Look for correct question forms (Have you walked...? Do you prefer...?) and genuine follow-up questions. In a small class or at the start of a session, let students use the same classmate twice or write "Nobody has... yet".

quests.title: Mayor for a Day
quests.text: Imagine the mayor of Pixel Plaza can add only one new thing: maybe a cinema, a skate park, an ice-cream stand, or your own idea. In a group of three or four, each person picks a different idea and tries to persuade the others. Explain where in the Plaza it would go and who it would help. Then negotiate one final choice. Useful phrases: "If we built..., people could...", "I see your point, but...", "What if we compromised and...?" Write a short paragraph summarising each person's proposal, the main arguments, and how your group reached its decision.
quests.teacherNote: Look for second conditionals (If we built..., it would...) and polite negotiation language. Groups can walk to the spot where they would put their idea while arguing, which makes their reasons more concrete.

quests.title: Festival Planners
quests.text: Plan a festival in Pixel Plaza: a chestnut festival (Castanyada), a friendly Halloween party, Saint George's Day, or another celebration you like. Mingle and ask at least four classmates for one activity idea each and where it should happen (the square, the cafe, the park...). Discuss the ideas and persuade people to support your favourites. Useful phrases: "The square would be perfect for... because...", "That might be too..., so how about...?" Write a short paragraph presenting your festival plan: the best ideas, where they go, where people disagreed, and why you chose them.
quests.teacherNote: The chat only accepts English, so students should type "chestnut festival" or "Saint George's Day" rather than Catalan names. Look for suggestions backed by reasons and a summary that includes at least one different opinion.

quests.title: Suitcase Trouble
quests.text: Imagine a tourist with a huge, heavy suitcase arrives at the hotel and wants to sit by the pond in the park. With a partner, each of you walks a different route and checks it: Is it short? Is it easy? Is anything in the way? Then compare your routes and agree on the best one. Useful phrases: "My route is longer, but it's much easier because...", "If the tourist went that way, they'd have to...", "On balance, I'd recommend..." Write a short paragraph giving clear directions for the best route and explaining why it is better than the other one.
quests.teacherNote: If there is only one obvious path, one partner can take a detour (for example past the cafe or across the square) so there is something to compare. Look for clear sequenced directions plus a balanced justification (longer but easier, shorter but busier).

quests.title: The Great Cake Mystery
quests.text: Solve a mystery: the cafe's prize-winning cake has disappeared! The suspects are a hungry seagull, a sleepy giant and a cake-loving robot. Mingle and interview at least four classmates as witnesses: "Where were you at the time, and what were you doing?" "What did you notice?" Witnesses can invent their stories, but they must stay consistent. Useful phrases: "It can't have been the... because...", "The ... must have...", "One witness claimed that..., whereas..." Write a short paragraph summarising the statements and explaining who you think took the cake.
quests.teacherNote: The suspects are fictional, so no classmate is ever accused; classmates are only witnesses. Look for must have / can't have / might have and past continuous in the witness answers, and reward students who spot contradictions between statements.

quests.title: Plaza Time Machine
quests.text: Imagine Pixel Plaza 100 years in the past or 100 years in the future. Walk with a partner to three places and discuss how each one might have looked then, or might look in the future. Would the cafe still exist? What would replace the shop? Challenge each other's ideas with follow-up questions. Useful phrases: "A hundred years ago, there would probably have been...", "In the future, this might become...", "I doubt it, because..." Write a short paragraph comparing your ideas and your partner's, and say which version of the Plaza you would rather visit and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for speculative language (might have been, would probably, could become) and a genuine comparison of two viewpoints. Weaker pairs can choose only the future, which needs simpler forms (will, might).

quests.title: Order Up!
quests.text: Go to the cafe with a classmate. You are the waiter. Say: "Can I help you?" Your classmate orders a drink and a snack. Write 2 sentences: "My classmate ordered ... and ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Listen for "Can I have ..., please?" and food and drink words. Students can invent items and should swap roles when finished.

quests.title: Drink Poll
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "What is your favourite drink?" Then write 2 sentences about their answers: "... likes ... ." Tell the chat your own favourite drink too.
quests.teacherNote: Good warm-up for mingling. Check that students use "likes" with the third person and ask the question in full.

quests.title: Tea and Cake
quests.text: Read: a tea is 2 euros. A cake is 3 euros. You buy a tea and a cake. How much is it? Type the number. Then ask a classmate the same question.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: 2 + 3 = 5. The prices are imaginary. The accepted phrases 5 and five also match answers like "5 euros" or "it is five".

quests.title: Shop Helper
quests.text: Visit the shop with a classmate. You are the shopkeeper. Say: "Can I help you?" Your classmate asks for a hat or a T-shirt in one colour. Write 2 sentences: "My classmate wants ... . The colour is ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Look for clothes and colour words. Students may use their avatar's hat or shirt as inspiration. Swap roles if time allows.

quests.title: Hotel Check-In
quests.text: Meet a classmate at the hotel. You are the receptionist. Use avatar names. Ask: "What is your name?" and "How many nights?" Write 2 sentences: "The guest is ... . The guest wants ... nights."
quests.teacherNote: Remind students to use avatar names or invented names, not real personal details. Swap roles if time allows.

quests.title: Wrong Drink
quests.text: Role-play this at the cafe with a classmate: you ordered a hot chocolate, but the waiter brought tea. Complain politely and ask for the right drink. Then swap roles. Useful phrases: "Excuse me, I asked for ..." "I'm sorry about that." Write 3 sentences: what happened and what the waiter said.
quests.teacherNote: Check for polite tone (Excuse me, please, sorry) and past simple (ordered, brought, asked).

quests.title: Too Small Jumper
quests.text: Go to the shop with a classmate. Yesterday you bought a jumper, but it is too small. Ask to change it. The shopkeeper asks: "What size do you want?" Swap roles. Useful phrases: "I bought this yesterday." "Can I change it?" Write 3 sentences about what you said.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for "Can I ...?", sizes (small, medium, large) and past simple. The jumper is imaginary.

quests.title: Lost Room Key
quests.text: Role-play at the hotel with a classmate. You are a guest and you lost your room key. Ask the receptionist for help. Useful phrases: "Could you help me?" "I lost it in ..." "I'm sorry to hear that." Swap roles. Write 3 sentences: where you lost the key and what the receptionist did.
quests.teacherNote: Look for "Could you help me?", past simple answers and receptionist questions such as "When did you lose it?". Students invent the story.

quests.title: Shopping Stories
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "What did you buy last time you went shopping?" and "Did you like it?" Real or invented answers are fine. Write 3 sentences about the most interesting answer. Use: "They bought ... . They liked it because ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Check did/didn't questions and irregular past forms (bought, went). Invented answers are explicitly allowed so nobody has to share personal details.

quests.title: Perfect Present
quests.text: Plan a birthday present for an imaginary friend. Go to the shop with two classmates. Each person suggests one present. Agree on one. Useful phrases: "How about ...?" "I think we should ..." "We are going to buy ..." Write 3 sentences: your choice and why.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for suggestions and agreement language. The friend is imaginary, so no personal information is needed.

quests.title: Dream Cafe Menu
quests.text: Create a menu for a dream cafe with two or three classmates. You need one drink, one snack and one special dish. Share ideas, give reasons, and agree on a cafe name and an imaginary price for each item. Useful phrases: "I'd put ... because ..." "Don't you think ... would be better?" Write 4 sentences about your final menu and why you chose it.
quests.teacherNote: Look for reasons with because/so and for negotiating language. Prices are invented only.

quests.title: Tourist Tips
quests.text: Role-play at hotel reception with a classmate. One of you is a tourist and the other is the receptionist. The tourist says what they like, for example quiet places, food or games. The receptionist asks follow-up questions and recommends two places in the plaza, with reasons. Useful phrases: "If you like ..., you should ..." "What kind of ... do you enjoy?" "It's better than ... because ..." Swap roles. Write 4 sentences about the advice you gave and got.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for first-conditional style advice (If you like ..., you should ...) and genuine follow-up questions. Places can be any part of the plaza: cafe, shop, fountain, park, pond or bridge.

quests.title: Souvenir Vote
quests.text: Imagine you run the plaza shop and must choose souvenirs for tourists. Ask four classmates which souvenir they would sell and why. Ask one follow-up question each time. Useful phrases: "What would you sell?" "Why do you think so?" "That's a good idea because ..." Write 4 sentences comparing two of the answers.
quests.teacherNote: Look for would-conditionals and real follow-up questions. Students may suggest anything from the plaza, the park or the town.

quests.title: Mystery Customer
quests.text: Secretly choose a funny customer, for example a sleepy robot or a pirate on holiday. Visit the cafe and order like that character, but never say who you are. Your partner asks questions and guesses. Swap. Useful phrases: "Are you ...?" "Do you usually ...?" "I think you are ... because ..." Write 3 or 4 sentences: who you guessed and the clues.
quests.teacherNote: Encourages questions and speculation. Characters should be fictional or fantasy, not real people.

quests.title: Welcome Gift Debate
quests.text: The hotel wants a free welcome gift for guests. With two classmates, compare three gifts, for example a map, a snack or a postcard. Decide which is more useful and which is better value. Useful phrases: "... is more useful than ..." "It's cheaper but ..." "In my opinion ..." Write 4 sentences with at least two comparisons.
quests.teacherNote: Check comparative forms (more useful than, cheaper than, better). Accept any three gifts the group chooses.

quests.title: Bulk Buy Bargain
quests.text: Negotiate a deal in a role-play with a classmate. A customer wants to buy twenty T-shirts for a school trip, but the shopkeeper does not want to lose money. Customer: ask for a discount, free delivery or a gift. Shopkeeper: protect your profit but keep a good customer. Keep talking until you both accept a compromise. Useful phrases: "I understand your position, however ..." "Would you be willing to ...?" "If you could ..., I'd be happy to ..." Swap roles. Write a short paragraph: the deal, what each side gave up, and whether both were happy.
quests.teacherNote: Look for diplomatic language, conditionals and a genuine compromise rather than one side giving in. Scenario and prices are fictional.

quests.title: Four Star Verdict
quests.text: Imagine a review of the plaza hotel: lovely staff, but expensive rooms and a small breakfast. With three classmates, each take a viewpoint: a business traveller, a family, a student group, or the manager. Discuss whether the hotel deserves four stars. Listen, disagree politely and try to reach a verdict. Write a paragraph summarising each viewpoint and your final decision, with reasons.
quests.teacherNote: Check that each viewpoint is represented and that students use concession language (although, on the other hand). The review is invented.

quests.title: Pitch a Shop
quests.text: Pitch an idea for one new shop in the plaza: what would it sell, and why would people visit? Meet two or three classmates. Each person pitches in two or three sentences and tries to persuade the others. Ask tough questions, such as "What if nobody comes?" Vote for the best idea, but not your own. Write a paragraph: which idea won, why it convinced you, and what could go wrong.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for second conditionals (would sell, if we opened) and persuasive language. Fun, unusual ideas are welcome as long as they stay kind.

quests.title: Phones at the Cafe
quests.text: Discuss this idea: some cafes ask customers to put their phones away while they eat. Ask at least four classmates whether they would like to visit such a cafe, and ask for their reasons. Find someone who disagrees with you and have a short, friendly debate. Write a paragraph summarising the different views and saying whether anyone changed your mind.
quests.teacherNote: Look for balanced summaries (some argued ... whereas others ...) and respectful disagreement. Keep it about opinions on the idea, not about individuals' phone habits.

quests.title: Overbooked Hotel
quests.text: Role-play an overbooked hotel in a group of three or four: two guests have booked the same last room. One person is the receptionist and the others are guests. Guests explain why they need the room, with invented reasons. The receptionist proposes solutions and compensation. Rotate roles if time allows. Write a paragraph: what was agreed, and what you would do differently if you were the receptionist.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasion, apologising professionally and conditionals (I would offer ... if ...). Rotate roles if time allows.

quests.title: Party Food Vote
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates: "What food do you want at our party?" Then write 2 sentences. Use: "Two classmates want ... . I want ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Look for the question form and want in the present simple. Students may name any food or drink, and the party can be any celebration they like.

quests.title: Meet at the Bridge
quests.text: Ask a classmate: "Where do we meet, at the fountain or at the bridge?" Then ask: "What time?" Write: "We meet at the ... at ... o'clock." Then walk there together!
quests.teacherNote: Check the question Where do we meet and simple clock times. Pairs can use other places in the plaza, such as the cafe or the shop.

quests.title: Plaza Rule Maker
quests.text: Think of one good rule for the plaza. Tell a classmate: "Please do not ... ." Ask: "Is it a good rule?" Write 1 sentence: "Our rule: Please do not ... because ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Expect rules like do not run, do not shout, do not drop rubbish. Keep rules kind and about behaviour, never about people.

quests.title: Park Game Choice
quests.text: Ask a classmate: "What game do you want to play in the park?" Answer the same question. Write 2 sentences: "I want to play ... . My classmate wants to play ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Check do/does and the third person s in wants. Any game is fine, such as tag, football, cards or hide and seek.

quests.title: Square Party Invitation
quests.text: Write an invitation for a party in the square. Use: "Come to my party on ... at ... . We have ... ." Send it to a classmate and ask: "Can you come?" Write your invitation in the journal.
quests.teacherNote: Look for a day, a time and one thing at the party. Any celebration is fine, such as a birthday, a game day or another festival.

quests.title: Lost in the Plaza
quests.text: Imagine you lost your bag in the plaza yesterday. Tell a classmate what it looked like, what was inside and where you lost it. Your classmate asks two questions. Then swap. Write 3 sentences. Useful phrases: "I lost my ... at the ...", "It was ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for past simple (lost, was) and colour, size and material words. The bag and its contents are invented, so nobody shares real belongings.

quests.title: Clean-Up Day Jobs
quests.text: Plan a clean-up day for the park. Choose 4 jobs, for example pick up rubbish. Ask your group which job each person wants. Write 3 sentences about who does which job. Useful phrases: "Who wants to ...?", "I'm going to ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check going to for plans and polite questions. Make sure every group member gets a job they chose.

quests.title: Fountain Show Time
quests.text: Solve this puzzle with a classmate. The fountain show in the square starts at 3 o'clock. It lasts 4 hours. The music stops 2 hours before the end. What time does the music stop? Type the time.
quests.teacherNote: The show ends at 7 o'clock, and two hours before that is 5 o'clock. Students may type the answer in digits or words.

quests.title: Market Stall Plan
quests.text: Plan a stall for the plaza market with a classmate. Decide the name of the stall and three things you are going to sell. Write 3 sentences. Useful phrases: "How about ...?", "Our stall is called ..."
quests.teacherNote: Items are imaginary, no real money needed. Look for suggestions with how about and agreement or disagreement.

quests.title: Best Party Ever
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates: "What was the best party or celebration you went to?" and "What did you do there?" Write 3 sentences about their answers. Useful phrases: "... went to ...", "They ate ..."
quests.teacherNote: Past simple is the focus, including irregular verbs such as went and ate. Students can talk about any celebration, not only birthdays, or choose not to share a real one and invent it.

quests.title: Park or Square
quests.text: Choose a place for a class picnic with a classmate: the park by the pond or the square by the fountain. Compare them, ask each other why, and try to agree. Write 4 sentences with your decision and reasons. Useful phrases: "It is more ... than ...", "I see your point, but ...", "Why do you prefer ...?"
quests.teacherNote: Listen for comparatives and polite disagreement. The decision matters less than the reasons they give.

quests.title: Visitor Top Three
quests.text: Plan one afternoon in the plaza for a visitor. Choose the three best things to do, for example cross the little bridge, have a drink at the cafe or sit by the fountain. Ask each person for a suggestion and a reason. Agree on the top three in order. Write 4 sentences. Useful phrases: "You should ...", "The best thing is ...", "I'd suggest ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for should, superlatives and clear reasons. Ask groups how they decided the order of their top three.

quests.title: Rain Plan B
quests.text: Make a Plan B with a classmate for an open-air film night in the square tomorrow. It might rain! Decide where to go and what to do instead. Write 4 sentences using if. Useful phrases: "If it rains, we will ...", "What if ...?"
quests.teacherNote: Check the first conditional: if plus present simple, then will. Plan B places can be the hotel, the cafe or the shop.

quests.title: Plaza Event Poll
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates which event they prefer for the plaza: a film night, a sports day or a food fair, or another idea. Ask follow-up questions to find out why. Write 4 sentences about the votes and reasons. Useful phrases: "Which do you prefer?", "Why do you think so?", "Can you tell me more?"
quests.teacherNote: Look for follow-up questions and reasons, not just votes. Students can suggest their own event if none of the three suits them.

quests.title: Talent Show Running Order
quests.text: Plan a talent show with five acts in your group. Invent the acts together. Decide the order: the loudest act cannot be first and the funniest act must be last. Agree and explain why. Write 5 sentences. Useful phrases: "First of all ...", "After that ...", "Finally ..."
quests.teacherNote: Listen for sequencing words and negotiation. The acts are invented, so the quest works without real talents.

quests.title: Plaza Music Rules
quests.text: Find a fair rule for the plaza. Some people want music all day. Others want quiet time. Ask three classmates for their views and their reasons. Then suggest one rule that could satisfy most people. Write a short paragraph summarising the views and explaining your rule. Useful phrases: "On the one hand ...", "A fair compromise would be ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for a balanced summary and a realistic compromise. Remind students to report views politely and not to judge classmates.

quests.title: Convince the Mayor
quests.text: One of you is the mayor, the other plans a big street party. The mayor asks tough questions about safety, noise and cost. The planner must convince the mayor. Swap roles if time allows. Write a short paragraph with the final decision and the strongest arguments. Useful phrases: "If we organised it, ...", "Would it be possible to ...?"
quests.teacherNote: Listen for hypothetical language, objections and answers. Costs stay imaginary. Rotate roles so quieter students also persuade.

quests.title: Everyone Welcome
quests.text: Imagine a plaza festival where everyone should feel welcome. Ask four classmates what could make an event more welcoming, for example food choices, different music or quiet areas. Compare their ideas. Write a short paragraph with your three best suggestions and the reasons. Useful phrases: "It would help if ...", "Not everyone ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for thoughtful reasons about different needs, such as diets, languages or celebrations. Keep ideas about events, not about named classmates.

quests.title: Budget Battle
quests.text: Your group has 100 imaginary coins to organise a plaza event. Choose a theme and decide how to spend the coins on four things such as food, music, decorations and prizes. Everyone must speak and compromise. Write a short paragraph explaining your budget and why. Useful phrases: "I'd rather spend more on ...", "Let's meet halfway."
quests.teacherNote: Coins are only for the game. Look for negotiation language, percentages or fractions, and reasons for each choice.

quests.title: Plaza in Ten Years
quests.text: Imagine the plaza in ten years. If you could add one permanent feature, what would it be? Ask four classmates for their ideas and compare them. Choose the idea you find most interesting. Write a short paragraph explaining what people said and why you picked it. Useful phrases: "If I could, I would ...", "It might be ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for would, might and reasoned comparison. Ideas can be playful, such as a skate park, a giant chessboard or a floating cafe.

quests.title: Hat Hunt
quests.text: Walk around and find 3 avatars with a hat. Ask them: "Do you like your hat?" Write 2 sentences like this: "... has a ... hat. ... likes it."
quests.teacherNote: Check that students use 'has' for the third person and put the colour before the noun ('a green hat'). If only a few avatars wear hats, let students ask about glasses instead.

quests.title: My Look, Your Look
quests.text: Tell a classmate about your avatar in nearby chat: "I have ... hair and a ... shirt." Ask: "And you?" Write 2 sentences: "I have ..." and "My classmate has ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for the change from 'I have' to 'my classmate has' and for the right word order ('a red shirt', not 'a shirt red'). Stronger students can add glasses or a hat.

quests.title: Colour Twins
quests.text: Walk around and find a classmate with the same shirt colour or hair colour as you. Ask: "Is your shirt ...?" Write: "My colour twin is ... . We both have ... ."
quests.teacherNote: This practises 'both' and colour words. If a student can't find an exact match, let them choose the closest colour ('We both have dark hair').

quests.title: Season Style
quests.text: Ask 2 classmates: "What do you wear in summer?" and "What do you wear in winter?" Write 2 sentences like this: "In winter, ... wears ... ." "In summer, ... wears ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Check 'wear' for I/you and 'wears' for the third person. Students talk about everyday clothes (coat, shorts, scarf), so no personal data is needed.

quests.title: Dream Hat
quests.text: Imagine a new hat for your avatar. Tell a classmate in nearby chat: "My dream hat is ... because ..." Then ask: "And you?" Write 1-2 sentences about your dream hat.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage two adjectives in the right order ('a big purple hat') and a simple reason with 'because'. Fast finishers can imagine their dream glasses too.

quests.title: Fountain Prize Puzzle
quests.text: Nora wears a red hat and no glasses. Pablo wears glasses and no hat. Kim has no hat and no glasses. Zoe wears a hat and glasses. The prize goes to the avatar with glasses but no hat. Who wins? Message a classmate: "It's ... because ..." Then type the name.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Pablo. He is the only avatar with glasses and no hat (Zoe has both, Nora has only a hat, Kim has neither). Students whisper their reason so they don't spoil the answer for others in nearby chat.

quests.title: Fashion Reporter
quests.text: Be a fashion reporter in the square. Ask 4 classmates about their avatars: "Why did you choose your hair colour?" and "What do you like best about your avatar?" Useful phrases: "I chose it because ...", "I like my ... best." Write 3 sentences: who you asked and what they said.
quests.teacherNote: Look for correct past simple questions ('Why did you choose...?') and the third person in the report ('Marc chose blue because...'). Remind reporters that every answer is a good answer.

quests.title: Hat or Glasses
quests.text: Ask 3 classmates a choice question. Example: "Which do you prefer, a big hat or funny glasses?" Then make your own choice question about colours or shirts. Useful phrases: "I prefer ... because ...", "Me too!" Write 3 sentences: who chose what and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for 'prefer', 'because' and correct 'which' questions. Students may invent their own choice questions, so check they stay about avatars and clothes.

quests.title: Party Look Planners
quests.text: Choose a celebration with 2 classmates: Halloween, the chestnut festival (Castanyada), Saint George's Day or another one you like. Plan your avatars' looks for it: hats, glasses, hair and shirt colours. Useful phrases: "I'm going to wear ...", "What are you going to wear?" Write 3 sentences: one about each person's look.
quests.teacherNote: Look for 'going to' and clothes and colour words. Festival names in answers should be in English (chestnut festival, Saint George's Day), and Halloween looks should stay fun, not scary.

quests.title: The Pixel Boutique
quests.text: Meet a classmate at the shop. One of you is the shop assistant; the other is a customer who wants a new hat or glasses. Useful phrases: "Can I help you?", "Have you got it in blue?", "It looks great!" Then swap roles. Write 3 sentences: what you wanted and what you chose.
quests.teacherNote: The shopping is pretend, so no game money or items are needed. Look for polite requests and past simple in the journal ('I wanted a red hat, but I chose a blue one').

quests.title: Cafe Colour Mystery
quests.text: Solve the puzzle. In the cafe, Ava, Ben, Cleo and Dan each wear a different shirt colour: red, blue, green or yellow. Dan's shirt is the same colour as a banana. Ava's shirt is neither red nor blue. Ben's shirt is neither red nor green. What colour is Cleo's shirt? Send your reasoning to a classmate. Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "So ... must be ..." Then type the colour.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: red. Dan is yellow (banana), so Ava must be green and Ben must be blue, which leaves red for Cleo. Ask students to explain it using 'must' and 'can't'.

quests.title: Plaza Fashion Awards
quests.text: Organise the Plaza Fashion Awards. Invent 2 positive categories, for example "Coolest Glasses" or "Most Colourful Avatar". Ask at least 4 classmates to vote in each category, then ask a follow-up question: "Why that one?" Useful phrases: "I'd vote for ... because ...", "For me, ... has the coolest ... because ..." Write 3-5 sentences: the winners and the best reasons people gave.
quests.teacherNote: Check superlatives (coolest, most colourful) and reasons that go beyond 'because it's nice'. Encourage many different categories so that lots of avatars win something and nobody is left out.

quests.title: Avatar Secret Lives
quests.text: Pick 2 avatars you can see in the square. Invent a job for each one, based on their look. For example: "That hat looks like a chef's hat, so this avatar might be a cook." Ask 2 classmates if they agree. Keep the ideas kind and fun. Useful phrases: "It might be ...", "Maybe, but it could also be ...", "I see why you think so." Write 3-5 sentences: your two avatars, their jobs and the best idea from your classmates.
quests.teacherNote: Look for 'might', 'could' and 'must' for speculation, plus polite disagreement. Ideas are about avatars' clothes only, never about real people, and must stay kind.

quests.title: Right Look, Right Place
quests.text: Compare your avatar with a classmate's avatar. Decide together whose avatar is better dressed for three situations: a picnic by the pond, a fancy party at the hotel and a rainy morning at the cafe. Give reasons and ask follow-up questions like "Why do you think so?" Useful phrases: "Your avatar is better dressed for ... because ...", "Mine is more ... than yours", "I see your point, but ..." Write 3-5 sentences comparing the two avatars.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives (brighter, more formal, better) and reasons linked to each situation. Keep it light: ideally each avatar wins at least one situation.

quests.title: Future Fashion 2100
quests.text: Imagine Pixel Plaza in the year 2100. What will avatars wear? Ask 2 or 3 classmates for their predictions about hats, glasses, hair and shirts, and ask a follow-up question about each idea. Useful phrases: "I think avatars will wear ...", "Maybe they won't need ... because ...", "Cool idea! Why ...?" Write 3-5 sentences: the best predictions and which idea you liked most, with a reason.
quests.teacherNote: Look for 'will/won't' for predictions and genuine follow-up questions. Groups that finish early can design one complete 2100 look together and post it in nearby chat.

quests.title: Team Parade Look
quests.text: Imagine your group of 3-4 is entering the Pixel Plaza Team Parade and needs one team look. Each person proposes a look (hair colour, hat, glasses, shirt colour) and tries to persuade the others. Then negotiate: you can combine ideas, but everyone must accept the final look. Useful phrases: "What if we ...?", "I could live with ... as long as ...", "Would you agree to ... if we ...?" Write a short paragraph: the proposals, the arguments that changed people's minds, and the final team look and team name.
quests.teacherNote: Look for negotiation language (conditionals, 'as long as', compromise) and a paragraph that reports different views, not just the final result. Make sure every member's proposal is heard.

quests.title: One Colour for All
quests.text: Debate an imaginary new law: "From next week, every avatar in Pixel Plaza must wear the same shirt colour." Is it fair, fun or a terrible idea? Ask at least 4 classmates what they think and why, and politely challenge each one with a "What if ...?" question. Useful phrases: "If this law existed, ...", "On the one hand ..., on the other hand ...", "Some people argued that ..., while others felt ..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and giving your own balanced opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Look for second conditionals ('If everyone wore red, ...') and a paragraph that reports several views fairly before giving an opinion. You can swap in another silly law, e.g. 'Glasses are banned at the pond'.

quests.title: Avatar Makeover Show
quests.text: Run a TV-style makeover show with a classmate. The host interviews the guest about their avatar: what they love about its look and what they would change if they could. Then the host suggests one makeover idea and tries to persuade the guest, who can accept, refuse or negotiate. Keep it kind. Swap roles. Useful phrases: "If you swapped your ... for ..., you'd ...", "Have you ever considered ...?", "I'm not sure that would suit my avatar because ..." Write a short paragraph: both makeover ideas, the arguments used, and whether each guest said yes.
quests.teacherNote: Look for tactful persuasion and conditionals ('If you swapped..., you'd...'). Remind hosts that the guest always decides, so a polite 'no thanks' is a good ending too.

quests.title: Riddle of the Square
quests.text: Write a riddle about one avatar you can see in the square (not your own) using creative clues instead of plain colour words, for example: "This avatar's hat is the colour of a ripe tomato, and its glasses would suit a famous detective." Send it to at least 4 classmates, one by one, and see who can guess the name. Keep every clue kind. Write a short paragraph: your riddle, how many classmates guessed it, which clue helped most, and what you would change if you did it again.
quests.teacherNote: Reward imaginative comparisons ('as bright as a traffic light', 'the colour of a ripe tomato') over plain colour words. Check that clues describe only the avatar's clothes and colours and are always kind.

quests.title: Launch Your Brand
quests.text: Invent a fashion brand for avatars, sold at the Pixel Plaza shop. Decide its name, a slogan and one signature item (a hat, glasses or a shirt), and think about who would wear it and where. Post your slogan in nearby chat and ask 2 classmates: "Would you buy this? What would make it better?" Useful phrases: "Imagine walking into the cafe wearing ...", "It's perfect for anyone who ...", "Unlike other brands, ours ..." Write a short paragraph pitching your brand and summarising the feedback you got.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive techniques (addressing the reader directly, 'Imagine...', contrast with 'unlike') and a fair summary of the feedback, including criticism. Brand names should be invented, not real ones.

quests.title: The Thumb Riddle
quests.text: Solve the riddle: "I have a thumb and four fingers, but I am not a hand. You wear me in winter." Type: "It is a ..." Then tell the riddle to a classmate.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: glove (it has a thumb and four fingers but is not a hand). A mitten is not accepted because it has no separate fingers. Extend by asking students to name more winter clothes, e.g. scarf, hat, coat.

quests.title: Head, Foot and Legs
quests.text: Find a partner. Read this riddle together: "I have a head, a foot and four legs, but I am not an animal. You sleep on me." Ask: "Is it a ...?" Type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: bed (a bed has a head, a foot and four legs). Point out the double meanings: the head and foot of a bed, the legs of a bed or table.

quests.title: Face and Hands
quests.text: Meet two or three classmates. Share this riddle: "I have a face and two hands, but no arms and no legs." Everyone writes: "I think it is a ..." Agree and type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: clock (watch is also accepted): it has a face and two hands. A good moment to review body words that also describe objects.

quests.title: Keys but No Doors
quests.text: Solve the riddle: "I have keys, but I open no doors. You play music on me." Then ask four classmates: "What am I?" Type the answer: "It is a ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: piano (keyboard, organ and accordion are also accepted, as they also have keys). Ask fast finishers to name other instruments in English.

quests.title: The Third Child
quests.text: Ask a classmate this riddle: "Tom's mum has three children. One is April. One is May. What is the name of the third child?" Read it slowly! Type: "The third child is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Tom. Many people say June because of April and May, but the answer is in the first word. Use it to revise the months and the possessive 's.

quests.title: Tea Time Puzzle
quests.text: Go to the cafe with a partner. Solve this riddle together: "What starts with T, ends with T and is full of T?" Hint: you can find it in the cafe. Useful phrases: "Maybe it's a ...", "No, because ...", "You're right!" Type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: teapot. It starts and ends with the letter T and is full of tea, which sounds like 'T'. Extension: pairs invent their own 'starts with... ends with...' riddle.

quests.title: Odd or Even?
quests.text: Solve this number riddle: "I am an odd number. Take away one letter from my name and I become even." Hint: spell the odd numbers in English: one, three, five... Then send the riddle to a classmate. Can they solve it? Type: "The number is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: seven (7): take away the S and 'seven' becomes 'even'. Check that students know 'odd' (1, 3, 5...) and 'even' (2, 4, 6...) before they start.

quests.title: Walk in the Park
quests.text: Go to the park with two or three classmates. Walk over the little bridge together. Then solve this riddle: "The more you take, the more you leave behind. What are they?" Hint: you took some on the bridge. Useful phrases: "I think they are ...", "Good idea!", "I don't agree." Type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: footsteps (steps and footprints are also accepted): the more steps you take, the more you leave behind you. Listen for agreeing and disagreeing phrases in the group chat.

quests.title: The Calendar Trap
quests.text: Ask four classmates this riddle: "Some months have 30 days and some have 31. How many months have 28 days?" Count how many classmates say "one". Then think again carefully! Useful phrases: "What's your answer?", "Are you sure?" Type: "... months have 28 days."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: all twelve months have at least 28 days; 'one' (February) is the trap. Follow up by asking how many classmates fell into the trap, e.g. 'Three people said one.'

quests.title: The Strange Room
quests.text: Solve this riddle: "I am a room, but I have no doors, no windows and no walls. Some people love me on pizza. What am I?" Then ask a classmate if they agree. Useful phrase: "I think it's a ... because ..." Type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: mushroom (the word ends in 'room', but it has no doors, windows or walls). Extension: ask students to find other words with a smaller word hidden inside, e.g. pancake, butterfly.

quests.title: Minute and Moment
quests.text: Solve this classic riddle: "What comes once in a minute, twice in a moment, but never in a thousand years?" Hint: don't think about time, think about spelling. When you know the answer, test it on a classmate in nearby chat and give hints if they get stuck. Useful phrases: "Have you noticed that ...?", "Look at the letters in ..." Type your answer as a full sentence: "It is the letter ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the letter M (one M in 'minute', two in 'moment', none in 'a thousand years'). Students must type 'the letter M' because a single letter cannot be checked safely, so a bare 'M' is not accepted.

quests.title: A Riddle for Two
quests.text: Send this riddle to a partner: "If you have me, you want to share me. If you share me, you don't have me anymore. What am I?" Discuss your ideas and give reasons. Which answer fits better, yours or your partner's? Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "I think it's ... because ...", "That makes sense!" Type the answer you agree on.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: a secret (once you share it, it is not a secret any more). If someone suggests 'a surprise', discuss why 'secret' fits better, and remind students not to share any real secrets in the chat.

quests.title: The Shrinking Word
quests.text: Solve this riddle: "Which five-letter English word becomes shorter when you add two letters to it?" Hint: think about what the longer word means. Then ask at least four classmates for their answers in nearby chat. Who found the trick first, and whose explanation is the clearest? Useful phrases: "What did you get?", "I think your idea is better because ..." Type: "The word is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: short (add -er and you get 'shorter'). Use it as a way into comparatives: ask students for other adjectives that take -er.

quests.title: Arriving on Friday
quests.text: Meet two or three classmates at the fountain. Discuss this riddle: "A cowboy rode into Pixel Plaza on Friday. He stayed at the hotel for three nights, and then he left on Friday. How is that possible?" Share ideas and ask follow-up questions. Useful phrases: "What if ...?", "Why do you think so?", "That can't be right because ..." Type one short sentence that explains the trick.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Friday is the name of the cowboy's horse, so he rode in on Friday and rode out on Friday. Any short sentence containing 'horse' is accepted; if groups get stuck, hint that 'on Friday' can have two meanings.

quests.title: Riddle Maker
quests.text: Write a "What am I?" riddle about something in Pixel Plaza, for example in the cafe, hotel, shop or park. Give three clues, from difficult to easy. Send it to a partner one clue at a time. After how many clues did they guess? Then swap roles. Useful phrases: "Here's my first clue: ...", "Do you want another clue?", "You got it!" Write 3-5 sentences: your riddle, your partner's guesses and the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Look for clear describing language (I am made of..., You use me to..., You can find me in...) and clues that really go from difficult to easy. Fast pairs can try a second riddle with only two clues.

quests.title: The Lobby Clock
quests.text: Solve this logic riddle, then challenge a classmate: "The old clock in the hotel lobby rings once for each hour, so it rings six times at six o'clock, with equal gaps between the rings. From the first ring to the last takes exactly five seconds. How long does it take from the first ring to the last at twelve o'clock?" Careful: the obvious answer is wrong. If a classmate disagrees with you, try to persuade them with a clear explanation. Useful phrases: "If six rings take ..., then ...", "The key point is that ..." Type the number of seconds.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 11 seconds. Six rings have five gaps (one second each); twelve rings have eleven gaps, so the answer is 11, not the 'obvious' 10.

quests.title: Fox, Chicken and Corn
quests.text: Meet a partner on the little bridge and solve this classic puzzle: "A farmer must take a fox, a chicken and a bag of corn across a river. Her boat carries her and only one of them. If she leaves the fox with the chicken, the fox eats it. If she leaves the chicken with the corn, the chicken eats it." Plan the trips together. Useful phrases: "What if she took ... first?", "That wouldn't work because ...", "If she took ..., the ... would ..." Type which one crosses the river most times in the shortest plan.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the chicken. Shortest plan (7 crossings): chicken over, farmer back, fox over, chicken back, corn over, farmer back, chicken over again. So the chicken crosses three times and the others once. Listen for 'If she took..., the ... would...'.

quests.title: Bankrupt at the Hotel
quests.text: Meet two or three classmates in the hotel and solve this lateral-thinking riddle: "A man pushes his car to a hotel. As soon as he arrives, he tells the owner that he is bankrupt (he has no money left). Why?" Hint: nobody is really sad, and the car is tiny. Take turns suggesting explanations and testing them. Before you decide, one person summarises the group's ideas. Useful phrases: "What if he were ...?", "That doesn't explain why ...", "So far, we think ..." Type one short sentence that explains what is really happening.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: he is playing Monopoly: his token is the little car, he lands on a street with a hotel and cannot pay the rent. Answers naming Monopoly or 'a board game' are accepted.

quests.title: Triple Double Trouble
quests.text: Work with at least four classmates in nearby chat to crack this word puzzle: "Which English word has three double letters in a row, like the made-up word aabbcc?" Hint: it is a job. This person keeps the money records of a business, such as a hotel. Everyone suggests words with double letters (coffee? balloon? committee?) and explains why each one does or doesn't work. Before you type, summarise which ideas you ruled out and why. Useful phrases: "That's close, but ...", "Let's rule out ...", "So far, we've found ..." Type the word.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: bookkeeper (oo-kk-ee); 'bookkeeping' also works. 'Coffee' (only two pairs in a row) and 'committee' (three pairs, but not in a row) are good near misses to discuss.

quests.title: Riddle Verdict
quests.text: Ask at least four classmates in nearby chat which kind of riddle they enjoy most: word riddles, logic puzzles, trick questions or lateral-thinking stories. Ask why, and whether riddles help them learn English. If someone disagrees with you, try to persuade them to try your favourite kind. Useful phrases: "Some people think ..., whereas others ...", "That's a fair point, but ...", "It depends on ..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views, and say which kind of riddle you would put on the Quest board for the whole class, and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for a real summary of several classmates' opinions (not just a list) and a reasoned recommendation using contrast and concession language. Replaces the earlier riddle-writing task so it does not repeat Riddle Maker.

quests.title: Secret Place Scramble
quests.text: Unscramble N-T-A-I-N-F-O-U to find a place in Pixel Plaza. Walk there and write in nearby chat: "I am at the ...!" Then type the place in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: fountain (in the square). Check the nearby chat to see who reached it; to reuse the quest, scramble another place, e.g. B-I-D-E-G-R (bridge).

quests.title: Cafe Odd One Out
quests.text: Find the odd one out: milk, juice, bread, water, tea. Ask two classmates in nearby chat: "Which word is different?" Say: "I think it is ..." Type the odd word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: bread, because it is food and the others are drinks. Fast finishers can add a reason with "because" in the chat.

quests.title: Opposite Animal Code
quests.text: Find the opposites of up, young and bad. Their first letters spell an animal. Ask a classmate: "What is the opposite of ...?" Type the animal in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: down, old, good, so the animal is DOG. Remind students to type the animal, not the three opposites (those alone are marked wrong).

quests.title: The Magic Word
quests.text: Find one word that goes after foot, basket and snow to make three new words. Ask a classmate: "What is your word?" Type the magic word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: ball (football, basketball, snowball); the three compound words are also accepted. Fast finishers can find more ball words, such as handball or volleyball, and share them in nearby chat.

quests.title: Class Fruit Salad
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "Can you name a fruit?" Every fruit must be different! Then write 1-2 sentences in your journal: "My class fruit salad has ..., ..., ... and ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check the spelling of the fruit names and that each one is different. Reuse the quest by changing the category to vegetables, animals or clothes.

quests.title: Hungry Word Chain
quests.text: Play a food word chain with two or three classmates in nearby chat. The next food must start with the last letter of the food before (apple, egg, grapes...). No repeats! Useful phrases: "Your turn!", "Is that a food?" Write 2-3 sentences: how many words your chain had and which word was the best.
quests.teacherNote: Read the nearby chat to check spelling and that each word follows the last-letter rule. For a harder version, ban plurals or change the topic to animals or countries.

quests.title: Rhyme Time
quests.text: Find three pairs of rhyming words with a classmate. Start with: cat, light, bear. Example: cat - hat. Useful phrases: "Does it rhyme with ...?", "I know one!" Write 3 funny sentences, one for each pair.
quests.teacherNote: Possible pairs: cat/hat, light/night, bear/chair. Accept rhymes by sound, not spelling, and praise funny sentences; ask students to read their rhymes aloud in class.

quests.title: Past Tense Tennis
quests.text: Play past tense tennis with a classmate in nearby chat. You write a verb, like "go". Your partner writes the past form, "went", and a new verb for you. Keep going! Useful phrases: "Is that right?", "Good one!" Write 2-3 sentences about yesterday with past verbs from your game.
quests.teacherNote: Check the past forms in the chat, especially irregular verbs (went, saw, ate, took). Make it harder by banning regular verbs or setting a 10-second limit.

quests.title: Hidden Animal Hunt
quests.text: Write the same three letters in each gap: VA___ION, EDU___ION, LO___ION. The three letters spell an animal! Ask four classmates in nearby chat: "Do you know the animal?" Type it in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: cat (vacation, education, location). Ask early finishers for more words with cat inside, such as catch, category or caterpillar.

quests.title: Ship to Stop
quests.text: Change one letter at a time to go from SHIP to STOP: SHIP, ?, STOP. The middle word is a place in Pixel Plaza. Then make your own ladder (like HOT, ?, CAT) and send it to a classmate. Useful phrase: "Is that a word?" Type the middle word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: SHOP (SHIP, SHOP, STOP); the only other route, STIP, is not a word, so the answer is unique. Check that students' own ladders change only one letter at each step.

quests.title: Prefix Detective
quests.text: Make the opposite of each adjective by adding a prefix: happy, kind, polite, friendly, fair. One word needs a different prefix from the others. Which one? Compare your answer with a classmate and explain your reasons. Useful phrases: "I think the odd one is ... because ...", "Do you agree?", "What about ...?" Type the odd adjective in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: polite, because its opposite is impolite while the others take un- (unhappy, unkind, unfriendly, unfair); impolite is also accepted. Extend with dis- and il- words such as dishonest and illegal.

quests.title: Listen Carefully
quests.text: Rearrange all the letters of LISTEN to make a new word that means "with no sound at all". Then go to the place in Pixel Plaza you think is the most peaceful and tell classmates nearby why. Useful phrases: "It's quieter than ...", "I prefer it because ..." Type the new word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: SILENT (the same six letters as LISTEN; silence is not accepted because it is not an anagram). Listen for comparatives in the chat; extra anagram pairs for fast finishers: EARTH/HEART, NIGHT/THING.

quests.title: The Wettest Riddle
quests.text: Solve this riddle: "What gets wetter and wetter the more it dries?" (Clue: you can find one in every hotel bathroom.) Before you type, ask at least four classmates in nearby chat for their guesses and ask follow-up questions to check their ideas. Useful phrases: "What's your guess?", "Why do you think that?", "That's clever, but ..." Type the answer in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: a towel (it dries you, so it gets wet). Only towel is accepted, so if students argue for a sponge, praise the reasoning and discuss why towel fits better.

quests.title: Sweet Idiom Puzzle
quests.text: Find the one food word that completes all three expressions: "a piece of ___" (very easy), "the icing on the ___" (the best extra thing) and "you can't have your ___ and eat it" (you can't have everything you want). Work with a classmate, then discuss which expression is the most useful and why. Useful phrases: "I'd use this one when ...", "I prefer ... because ..." Type the food word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: cake (a piece of cake, the icing on the cake, you can't have your cake and eat it). Listen for the idioms used in real examples, and follow up with other food idioms such as "spill the beans".

quests.title: Mystery Word
quests.text: Play "Mystery Word" with two or three classmates. One player secretly chooses an object from Pixel Plaza, like something in the cafe or the park. The others ask yes/no questions in nearby chat to guess it, with a maximum of 15 questions. Take turns. Useful phrases: "Is it bigger than ...?", "Can you eat it?", "Is it used for ...?" Write 3-5 sentences: which words you guessed, how many questions it took, and which question helped most. During each round, the clue-giver answers yes or no without naming the object. Guessers may name their guesses; confirm a correct guess with yes, then swap.
quests.teacherNote: Look for correctly formed yes/no questions and comparatives in the chat. Make it harder with a 10-question limit or a ban on colour questions. Student-chosen secrets are not registered in the app, so these round rules need teacher review; there is no automatic word block for this quest.

quests.title: The Shrinking Word (Word Games)
quests.text: Solve this riddle with two or three classmates: "Which five-letter word becomes shorter when you add two letters to it?" Each person suggests an answer in nearby chat and tries to persuade the others it is right. If you disagree, explain your reasoning and listen to the other arguments before you decide together. Think about the meaning of the riddle, not only the spelling. Useful phrases: "I'm convinced it's ... because ...", "That's a fair point, but ...", "What if the answer is ...?" Type your group's answer, the five-letter word, in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: SHORT, because short + er = shorter. Listen for persuasion and polite disagreement; groups that finish early can invent a similar riddle for another group.

quests.title: One Small Word
quests.text: Find the one small word that completes all three sentences: "We've run ___ of milk, so I'll buy some at the shop." "Can you help me work ___ the answer to this puzzle?" "I was shocked when I found ___ the truth." Message a classmate to compare answers. Then each of you writes one more sentence with a phrasal verb using the same word; decide together which sentence sounds more natural and why. Useful phrases: "I'd say it's ... because ...", "Wouldn't ... sound more natural?" Type the missing word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: out (run out of, work out, find out); "on" fits the second sentence but not the first, which makes a good discussion point. Check the extra sentences for natural phrasal verbs such as sort out, go out or check out.

quests.title: Three Meanings, One Word
quests.text: Find one English word with all three of these meanings: a season of the year; a place where water comes up naturally out of the ground; and a metal coil that jumps back when you press it. When you have it, invent a similar three-meaning clue for another word with several meanings (for example "light", "match" or "bat") and send it to a classmate. If they guess it, ask which meaning they found easiest and why. Useful phrases: "Here's a tricky one for you...", "Which meaning gave it away?" Type the word with three meanings in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: spring (the season, a water spring, a metal spring). Check that the clues students post have only one answer; good models are match (a game, a fire stick, to go well together) and light (not heavy, not dark, a lamp).

quests.title: Desert Island Dictionary
quests.text: Imagine your group is on a desert island and can only keep five English words; every other word disappears forever. With two or three classmates, negotiate in nearby chat which five words to keep. Each person proposes two words and tries to persuade the others, then you must agree on a final list. Useful phrases: "If we lost ..., we couldn't ...", "I see your point, but ...", "Shall we compromise on ...?" Write a short paragraph: your final five words, the best argument you heard, and one word you were sad to lose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for second conditional sentences, persuasion and compromise in the chat. Adapt it by limiting the list to verbs or adjectives, or by changing the number of words.

quests.title: New Words for Pixel Plaza
quests.text: Invent a new compound word for something in Pixel Plaza that has no name yet, for example "lift-wait" (the feeling of waiting ages for the hotel lift) or "fountain-walker" (someone who walks round the fountain all day). Write it with a hyphen and keep it kind: never name a classmate. Explain your word to at least four classmates in nearby chat, listen to theirs and vote for the best one. Useful phrases: "It would be perfect for ...", "Mine is catchier because ...", "Yours is clever, but ..." Write a short paragraph: your word and its meaning, the best word you heard, and why it got your vote.
quests.teacherNote: Check that invented words are kind and not aimed at real classmates. If the chat filter blocks a new word, students can type the two parts separately (lift wait).

quests.title: Day Counting
quests.text: Solve this: today is Monday. What day is it in five days? Write: "It is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Monday plus five days is Saturday. Good quick warm-up for days of the week.

quests.title: Apple Count
quests.text: Solve this puzzle with a classmate. You have 8 apples. You give 3 to Ana and 2 to Ben. How many apples do you have now? Write: "I have ... apples."
quests.teacherNote: 8 - 3 - 2 = 3. Students should talk with their partner in English to agree on the answer.

quests.title: Letter Code
quests.text: Use this code: A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, D = 4. What number is B + A + D? Write: "The answer is ..."
quests.teacherNote: B + A + D = 2 + 1 + 4 = 7. Students can then invent their own code word and whisper it to a friend.

quests.title: Who Sits Where
quests.text: Solve: three friends sit in a row, Ana, Ben and Cam. Ana does not sit next to Cam. Who sits in the middle? Ask two classmates. Write: "... sits in the middle."
quests.teacherNote: Ana and Cam cannot be neighbours, so they sit at the ends and Ben must be in the middle.

quests.title: Lucky Numbers
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "What is your lucky number?" Then add the four numbers. Write 2 sentences: "My classmates' numbers are ..." "The total is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check that students report four numbers and a total. Any numbers are fine, so check the addition if you like.

quests.title: Twice As Old
quests.text: Solve this puzzle with a classmate. Maria is twice as old as her brother Tom. Together, they are 18 years old. How old is Maria? Useful phrases: "Let's try ...", "I think it is ...". Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: Tom is 6 and Maria is 12 (6 + 12 = 18). Students can find it by trying numbers.

quests.title: Juice Puzzle
quests.text: Solve this cafe puzzle: a juice and a sandwich cost 7 coins together. The sandwich costs 5 coins more than the juice. How much is the juice? Ask two classmates what they think. Useful phrases: "I think ...", "Let's check: ...". Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: The juice costs 1 coin and the sandwich 6 coins (6 - 1 = 5, 6 + 1 = 7). Many students first say 2, which is a good thing to discuss.

quests.title: Bus To The Park
quests.text: Work out the time. The bus leaves the square at 9:45. The trip to the park takes 35 minutes. What time does the bus arrive? Ask a classmate to check. Write: "It arrives at ..."
quests.teacherNote: 9:45 plus 35 minutes is 10:20. Accepted forms include 10:20, ten twenty and twenty past ten.

quests.title: Jumping Frogs
quests.text: Find the pattern: the frogs by the pond jump 3, 6, 12, 24 ... What number comes next? Ask four classmates if they find the same pattern. Useful phrases: "Each number is ...", "The next number is ...". Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: The numbers double each time, so the next is 48. The differences (3, 6, 12) also double, which gives the same answer.

quests.title: Hat Mix-Up
quests.text: Solve the puzzle with two classmates. Ali, Bea, Carl and Dina wear different hats: red, blue, green and yellow. Bea wears blue. Ali does not wear red or blue. Carl does not wear red or green. Who wears the red hat? Useful phrases: "It cannot be ...", "So ... wears ...". Type the name.
quests.teacherNote: Bea is blue. Carl cannot be red, green or blue, so he is yellow. Ali cannot be red or blue, so he is green. Dina is red.

quests.title: Fountain Benches
quests.text: Solve this seating puzzle with two classmates. Five friends sit on five benches numbered 1 to 5 from left to right: Mia, Leo, Zoe, Sam and Kai. Zoe sits on bench 3. Leo sits next to Zoe, on her left. Sam sits on bench 5. Mia does not sit next to Leo. Who is on bench 1? Useful phrases: "That means ...", "It can't be ... because ...". Type the name.
quests.teacherNote: Zoe is 3, Leo is 2, Sam is 5. Mia and Kai take benches 1 and 4. Mia cannot be next to Leo (bench 2), so Mia is 4 and Kai is 1.

quests.title: The Cake Thief
quests.text: Find the cake thief. One of three friends ate the last cake in the cafe. Only ONE of these statements is true. Ana says: "Ben ate it." Ben says: "I did not eat it." Cleo says: "Ana is lying." Who ate the cake? Discuss with a classmate. Useful phrases: "If ... is true, then ...", "That is a contradiction." Type the name.
quests.teacherNote: Ana's and Cleo's statements contradict each other, so exactly one is true. Ben's statement must therefore be false, so Ben ate the cake. Check: Ana true, Ben false, Cleo false.

quests.title: Bell Tower Count
quests.text: Work out the answer. The clock tower in the square rings once at 1 o'clock, twice at 2 o'clock, three times at 3 o'clock, and so on. How many rings are there from 1 o'clock to 4 o'clock, including both? Ask four classmates to check your answer and compare methods. Useful phrases: "First I ...", "Then I added ...". Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. Encourage students to explain their method with sequencing words.

quests.title: Mystery Number
quests.text: Find the secret number with your group. Each person reads one clue in the chat. Clue 1: it is between 10 and 60. Clue 2: it is a multiple of 7. Clue 3: its two digits add up to 8. What is the number? Useful phrases: "Let's list the multiples of 7", "That does not work because ...". Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: Multiples of 7 between 10 and 60: 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56. Only 35 has digits that add up to 8 (3 + 5).

quests.title: Secret Cafe Code
quests.text: Decode this message with a classmate. Each letter is written one step later in the alphabet, so A is written as B. The message is: UIF DBGF JT PQFO. Type the decoded message in English. Then, if you have time, send your own coded message to your partner and see if they can decode it.
quests.teacherNote: Shift each letter back by one: UIF = THE, DBGF = CAFE, JT = IS, PQFO = OPEN. The answer is THE CAFE IS OPEN. The optional extension is not checked.

quests.title: Hotel Room Riddle
quests.text: Solve this hotel puzzle with your group. The Plaza hotel has four rooms in a row, numbered 1 to 4. Ivy, Jon, Kim and Lou each stay in a different room. Read one clue each in the chat. 1) Ivy is not in room 1 or room 4. 2) Jon is in an end room. 3) Kim is not next to Jon. 4) Kim is next to Lou. 5) Lou is not in room 4. 6) Ivy's room number is lower than Kim's. Who is in room 3? Explain your reasoning, then type the name.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: Jon 1, Ivy 2, Lou 3, Kim 4. If Jon is in room 4, Kim must be 1 or 2, which breaks clue 6 or clue 1; if Jon is in room 1, clues 3 to 6 force Ivy 2, Lou 3, Kim 4. The solution is unique.

quests.title: Truth And Lies
quests.text: Decide who tells the truth. Nia, Omar and Pia are each either a truth-teller, who always tells the truth, or a liar, who always lies. Nia says: "Omar is a liar." Omar says: "Pia is a liar." Pia says: "Nia and Omar are both liars." Discuss with a classmate and test each possibility, for example "If Nia is telling the truth, then ...". Who is the only truth-teller? Type the name.
quests.teacherNote: If Nia is honest, Omar lies, so Pia is honest, but then Nia would be a liar: contradiction. So Nia lies, Omar is honest and Pia lies. Omar is the only truth-teller.

quests.title: Torch On The Bridge
