quests.text: Plan a night crossing with your group. Four friends must cross the little bridge in the park. They have one torch, and the bridge holds only two people at a time. Ana crosses in 1 minute, Ben in 2, Cy in 5 and Dee in 10. Two people together go at the slower speed, and someone must carry the torch back. Try to convince your group that your plan is the fastest and listen to other ideas. What is the shortest total time in minutes? Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: Best plan: Ana and Ben cross (2), Ana returns (1), Cy and Dee cross (10), Ben returns (2), Ana and Ben cross (2). Total 17. The common wrong answer is 19.

quests.title: Party Handshakes
quests.text: Imagine a party where 8 people each shake hands once with every other person. How many handshakes are there in total? Do not just guess. Ask at least four classmates to help you test smaller groups first, for example 2, 3 and 4 people, and look for a pattern. Then compare your methods and decide which one is the quickest. Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: 8 x 7 / 2 = 28, or 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 28. Encourage students to explain the small-group pattern (1, 3, 6, 10 ...).

quests.title: Puzzle Makers
quests.text: Invent your own short logic puzzle in English with exactly one correct answer, for example about ages, seats or time. Send it by direct message to two classmates and see if they can solve it without help. Ask them which clue was hardest and how you could improve it. Write a short paragraph: your puzzle, the solution, what your classmates said, and one thing you would change.
quests.teacherNote: Check that the puzzle really has one solution and that the student reports real feedback. Good puzzles can be reused as class warm-ups.

quests.title: Pumpkin Chat
quests.text: Ask a classmate: 'Do you like pumpkin soup?' Then write 2 sentences: 'My classmate likes ... because ...' and 'I like ... because ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Accept 'does not like' answers too. Check students use 'because' with a simple reason.

quests.title: Autumn Colours
quests.text: Ask three classmates: 'What is your favourite autumn colour?' Write 2 sentences with the answers. Use: '... likes orange.' or '... likes red.'
quests.teacherNote: Quick mingle. Look for third-person -s ('Ana likes red'). Colours of avatars' clothes can help students start.

quests.title: Ghost Or Cat
quests.text: Choose a costume for your avatar, for example a ghost or a cat. Tell a classmate. Write: 'My avatar is a ... I like it because ...'
quests.teacherNote: Students may pick a costume for any celebration they like. Look for 'a/an' and a simple reason.

quests.title: Orange Riddle
quests.text: Solve the riddle: It is orange and round. At Halloween, people cut a face in it. What is it? Type one word.
quests.teacherNote: The answer is pumpkin. Students can ask classmates for help in the chat.

quests.title: Autumn Clothes
quests.text: Ask two classmates: 'What do you wear in autumn?' Write 2 sentences: '... wears a ... in autumn.' and 'I wear a ... in autumn.'
quests.teacherNote: Check clothing vocabulary (jacket, scarf, boots) and the -s on 'wears'.

quests.title: Autumn Food Poll
quests.text: Ask four classmates: 'What autumn food do you like?' Chestnuts, panellets and pumpkin soup are some ideas, or choose food from another celebration. Write 3 sentences about the answers. Useful phrases: 'Two people like ...', 'Nobody likes ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Students should name foods in English (chestnuts, sweet potato, pumpkin soup). Check quantity phrases such as 'two people', 'nobody'.

quests.title: Spooky Story Chain
quests.text: Make a funny spooky story with two or three classmates. Each person writes one sentence in the chat, in the past simple. Start: 'Last night, a ghost came to the cafe.' Then write the story in your journal, 3 sentences.
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple forms (came, saw, ran). Remind students the story should be funny, not scary.

quests.title: Ghost Tour Guide
quests.text: Plan a funny ghost tour with a partner. Choose three places in Pixel Plaza. Tell your partner how to walk from the fountain to each place. Write 3 sentences. Useful phrases: 'First, go to ...', 'Then turn left ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Look for direction words (left, right, straight on, over the bridge). Both partners should give directions.

quests.title: Halloween Date
quests.text: Halloween is the night before 1 November. What is the date of Halloween? Type the day and the month. Ask a classmate if you are not sure.
quests.teacherNote: The answer is 31 October. Both British and American date orders are accepted.

quests.title: Weather Reporter
quests.text: Be a weather reporter with a partner. Invent the autumn weather for tomorrow in Pixel Plaza. Take turns and use 'going to'. Write 3 sentences. Useful phrases: 'Tomorrow it is going to rain.', 'You are going to need ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Check 'be going to' forms and weather words (windy, foggy, cloudy). Encourage a funny reporter voice.

quests.title: Costume Showdown
quests.text: Your group needs one matching costume idea for a party, Halloween or another celebration you like. Each person suggests one idea and gives a reason. Ask each other follow-up questions, then vote. Write 3-5 sentences: the ideas, the winner and why. Useful phrases: 'I think ... because ...', 'What about ...?', 'I agree, but ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Look for reasons with 'because' and polite disagreement. A group of three avoids tied votes.

quests.title: Autumn Or Summer
quests.text: Interview a partner: which season is better, autumn or summer? Ask at least three questions, including one follow-up question. Compare your answers. Write 3-5 sentences. Useful phrases: 'Autumn is cosier than ...', 'Why do you think that?', 'We both ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Check comparative forms (cosier, more relaxing, better than) and that at least one real follow-up question was asked.

quests.title: Costume Shop Role-play
quests.text: Role-play with a partner in the shop. One of you is the shopkeeper, one is a customer who needs a Halloween costume for a party tomorrow. Ask about colours, sizes and ideas, then agree on a costume. Swap roles if you have time. Write 3-5 sentences about what happened. Useful phrases: 'Could I see ...?', 'I'd recommend ...'.
quests.teacherNote: No real money is involved. Look for polite requests and recommendations, and past simple in the written summary.

quests.title: Festival Reporter
quests.text: Ask four classmates about their favourite autumn or winter celebration. Find out what they do, eat or wear, and ask one follow-up question each. Write 3-5 sentences comparing their answers. Useful phrases: 'What do you usually do?', 'Why do you like it?', 'Most people ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Any celebration is fine, which keeps it inclusive. Look for present simple for habits and comparing language.

quests.title: Costume Logic
quests.text: Mia, Leo and Sam wear a witch hat, a cat mask and a ghost sheet. Mia wears no hat and no mask. Leo does not wear the mask. Who wears the cat mask? Talk about it with a classmate, then type the name.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: Mia must wear the ghost sheet, so Leo wears the hat, and Sam wears the cat mask.

quests.title: Plaza Festival Pitch
quests.text: Your group is the Pixel Plaza festival committee. Plan one autumn festival day with three activities. Each person pitches an idea and explains why it would be popular. Negotiate: you may only keep three ideas, so persuade, compromise and make sure everyone is happy with the result. Write a short paragraph explaining your final plan and why you chose those activities. Useful phrases: 'The main advantage is ...', 'I see your point, but ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive language, compromise and a clear justification. Ideas can come from any tradition.

quests.title: Borrowed Traditions
quests.text: Ask at least four classmates: 'Is it a good idea to celebrate festivals that come from other countries, like Halloween?' Ask each person for a reason and politely challenge one answer. Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and say which you agree with most, and why. Useful phrases: 'On the one hand ...', 'Some people argue that ...'.
quests.teacherNote: Keep the discussion about traditions and fun, not religion or politics. Look for contrast linkers and balanced summaries.

quests.title: Haunted Hotel Night
quests.text: Imagine the Pixel Plaza hotel is haunted in a friendly, funny way. Ask your partner: 'If you stayed there for a night, what would you do?' and 'What would you be most worried about?' Follow up with 'Why?' Then swap. Write a short paragraph comparing what you would each do, using 'would' and 'if'.
quests.teacherNote: Check second conditional accuracy (if I stayed, I would ...). Keep the mood light and silly.

quests.title: Cafe Menu Makeover
quests.text: You and a partner run the Pixel Plaza cafe and must create a new four-item autumn menu. You disagree: each person wants different dishes. Persuade each other with reasons, give way on some points and agree on the final menu. Write a short paragraph describing the menu and how you reached a compromise. Useful phrases: 'If we included ..., customers would ...', 'How about a compromise?'.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasion, conditionals and compromise phrases. Dishes can be from any culture or celebration.

quests.title: Missing Pumpkin Mystery
quests.text: Someone has taken the giant pumpkin from the fountain! With two or three classmates, invent theories about who did it and how, using 'must have', 'might have' and 'can't have'. Discuss each other's clues, question weak points and decide on the most likely explanation. Write a short paragraph summarising the theories and your group's final decision.
quests.teacherNote: Check modals of past deduction. Remind students not to blame a real classmate, only invented characters or funny ghosts.

quests.title: Snowman Riddle
quests.text: Read the riddle. I am white and cold. I have a carrot nose and a hat. What am I? Ask a classmate to guess too. Type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: The answer is a snowman. Students can compare guesses in the chat before typing.

quests.title: Snow or Rain
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "Do you like snow or rain?" Write 2 sentences: "... likes snow." "... likes rain."
quests.teacherNote: Check that students use the third person -s (likes). Weak groups can copy the frame exactly.

quests.title: Hot Winter Food
quests.text: Ask a classmate: "What is your favourite winter food?" Write 1 sentence: "My classmate likes ... because it is ... ." Use words like hot, sweet or tasty.
quests.teacherNote: Any food is fine, including food from other celebrations. Look for a correct because clause.

quests.title: Present for a Friend
quests.text: Think of a nice present for a friend. Tell a classmate in the chat. Write 1 sentence: "I want to give ... because ... ." Use any celebration or a birthday.
quests.teacherNote: Gifts are imaginary, so no money talk is needed. Encourage students to share with a classmate and react kindly.

quests.title: New Year Wishes
quests.text: Ask two classmates: "What is your wish for the new year?" Write 2 sentences: "... wishes for ... ." A wish can be about school, sport, friends or fun.
quests.teacherNote: Keep wishes light and positive. Students who do not celebrate New Year can wish for anything good.

quests.title: Snow Day Plan
quests.text: Imagine tomorrow is a snow day and school is closed. Ask a partner: "What are you going to do?" Then make a plan together. Write 3 sentences. Useful phrases: "We are going to ...", "First, we ...", "Then, we ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for going to plus a verb and sequencing words. Plans can use the plaza places.

quests.title: Last Winter Celebration
quests.text: Ask two classmates about a winter celebration they had last year. It can be Christmas, New Year, or any celebration you like. Use past simple. Useful phrases: "What did you eat?", "Who did you see?", "It was ..." Write 3 sentences about what they told you.
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple forms (ate, saw, was). Students may choose any celebration and need not share private details.

quests.title: Cafe Role-Play
quests.text: Role-play in the cafe with a partner. One is the waiter and one is the customer. Order a hot winter drink and a snack. Then swap roles. Write 2 sentences: what you ordered and what you liked. Useful phrases: "Can I have ...?", "Anything else?"
quests.teacherNote: Students practise Can I have and polite service language. Hot chocolate, tea and soup are all good choices.

quests.title: Resolution Round
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "What is your New Year resolution?" Reply kindly, for example "Good idea!" Any small goal is fine. Write 3 sentences. Useful phrases: "... is going to ...", "I am going to ..."
quests.teacherNote: Goals should be small and light (sport, hobbies, school). Check going to with the correct person form.

quests.title: Winter Outfit Designer
quests.text: Design a winter outfit for your avatar: a hat, a scarf, a jumper and shoes. Tell a classmate in the chat and ask: "Do you like it?" Write 3 sentences describing the outfit and the colours.
quests.teacherNote: Only avatars are described, never real people. Look for clothing vocabulary and colour adjectives in the right order.

quests.title: Best Winter Celebration
quests.text: Talk in a group of three or four. Which winter celebration is the best: Christmas, New Year, Three Kings' Day, or another one you like? Everyone gives an opinion and a reason, then asks one follow-up question. Write 3-5 sentences: what people chose and why. Useful phrases: "In my opinion ...", "That is true, but ...", "Why do you think so?"
quests.teacherNote: The open choice includes students who do not celebrate Christmas. Listen for reasons and polite disagreement.

quests.title: Winter Cafe Menu
quests.text: Plan a menu for a winter cafe with your group. Choose one hot drink, one soup or main dish, and one dessert. Compare ideas and agree on the final menu. Write 3-5 sentences: what you chose and why it is good for cold weather. Useful phrases: "How about ...?", "I would rather ...", "It is warmer than ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for suggestions, comparatives and a real agreement. Students can use food from any culture.

quests.title: Perfect Present Detective
quests.text: Ask a partner three questions about their hobbies and favourite things. Then suggest an imaginary present for them and explain why it is perfect. Your partner says if they agree. It can be for any celebration or just a surprise. Write 3-5 sentences. Useful phrases: "What do you do in your free time?", "I think you would love ... because ...", "That would be great!"
quests.teacherNote: Presents are imaginary and have no price. Check question forms and the reason after because.

quests.title: Goal Coach
quests.text: Ask a partner about one small goal for the new year, such as sport, a hobby or school. Ask two follow-up questions, then give one piece of advice. Write 3-5 sentences about the goal and your advice. Useful phrases: "What is your goal?", "How are you going to do it?", "You should ..."
quests.teacherNote: Students should keep goals small and non-personal. Look for follow-up questions and should plus verb.

quests.title: Snow or Sun
quests.text: Ask four classmates: would you prefer a winter holiday in snowy mountains or somewhere warm? Ask why, and ask one follow-up question each. Compare their answers. Write 3-5 sentences, using comparatives. Useful phrases: "I would rather ...", "... is more fun than ...", "Why is that?"
quests.teacherNote: This is an imaginary holiday, so no travel or money talk is needed. Check comparatives such as colder, more relaxing and better.

quests.title: Plaza Winter Tradition
quests.text: Invent a brand-new winter tradition for Pixel Plaza that any student could enjoy, whatever they celebrate. In your group, each person suggests an idea and a place for it: the square, park, cafe, hotel or shop. Persuade each other, negotiate changes, and vote. Write a short paragraph: describe the winning tradition, why it includes everyone, and one compromise you made.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive language, compromise phrases and inclusive thinking. Traditions should be new and secular or general.

quests.title: Presents or Time
quests.text: Ask three or four classmates this question: at a winter celebration, would you rather give a gift or spend time together, such as a game or a meal? Ask them to justify their view and respond politely to disagreement. Write a short paragraph summarising the different views, who agreed, and what you think after hearing them.
quests.teacherNote: Check that students report views accurately (some said, others argued) and give their own conclusion. Works for any celebration.

quests.title: Snowed In
quests.text: Imagine it snows for a whole week in Catalonia and everything closes. With a partner, discuss what would happen and what you would do. Use second conditional questions, for example "If we were stuck in the hotel, what would we do?" Write a short paragraph: three what-if sentences, your partner's best idea, and one thing neither of you could live without that week.
quests.teacherNote: Check if + past simple, would + verb. Funny ideas are welcome if the grammar is accurate.

quests.title: Time Capsule 2036
quests.text: Imagine a New Year time capsule that opens in ten years. Ask a partner what two things they would put inside and why, and say what you would choose. Discuss whether technology or traditions will change more. Write a short paragraph comparing your choices, using phrases like "If I could keep only one thing ..." or "Whereas you chose ..."
quests.teacherNote: Objects should be general, not private. Look for contrast linkers (whereas, however) and future predictions.

quests.title: Coziest Spot Campaign
quests.text: Each person in your group chooses a place in Pixel Plaza, such as the hotel, cafe, shop, square or park, and persuades the others it is the best place for a cold winter evening. Give two reasons and answer one objection. Then rank all the places together, negotiating when you disagree. Write a short paragraph: your ranking, the strongest argument you heard, and one point you changed your mind about.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive structure and respectful rebuttals. If the group is small, two places can be compared.

quests.title: Guess My Costume
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Think of a carnival costume. Don't tell! Your partner asks questions like "Are you a pirate?" Answer "Yes, I am" or "No, I'm not." Then swap. Write: "My partner is a ..."
quests.teacherNote: Listen for "Are you a ...?" and the short answers. If a pair gets stuck, allow category hints like "It's an animal."

quests.title: Ice Cream Survey
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "What ice cream do you like in summer?" Answer the question too. Which flavour is the winner? Write: "... classmates like ... and my favourite is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Expect flavours like chocolate, vanilla, strawberry and lemon. Teach "flavour" if needed, and check "like" after plural subjects ("Two classmates like...").

quests.title: Spring Word Race
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Meet two or three classmates in the park. Take turns in the chat: say one spring word, like "flower" or "rain". No repeats! Can you get ten? Then write: "Our spring words are ..."
quests.teacherNote: Expect words like sun, flowers, birds, rain, trees and butterflies. For a harder round, allow only adjectives, or only words that start with one letter.

quests.title: Pack for Camp
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Imagine you go to summer camp. Ask a classmate: "What is in your bag?" Answer too. Pack one funny thing! Write: "My partner's bag has a ..., a ... and a ..."
quests.teacherNote: Help with camp words (torch or flashlight, sleeping bag, tent, toothbrush, sun cream) and enjoy the funny items. Check "has" in the sentence they write.

quests.title: Fire and Wings Riddle
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Read the riddle: "I am big and green. I have wings and I breathe fire. Saint George fights me. What am I?" Ask a classmate to guess too. Type: "You are a ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: dragon. It is the creature in the Saint George's Day (Sant Jordi) legend, so this is a quick way into the story.

quests.title: Easter Break Plans
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "What are you going to do in the Easter break or spring holidays?" Then ask one more question, like "Where?" or "Why?" Plans at home are great too! Useful phrases: "I'm going to ...", "That sounds fun!" Write 3 sentences: who you asked and their plans.
quests.teacherNote: Check "going to + verb" in the reports (e.g. "Pau is going to visit his cousins"). Students with no plans can describe a relaxing week at home or make up a dream plan.

quests.title: The Costume Shop
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Go to the shop with a partner. One of you is the shop assistant; the other wants a carnival costume. Ask about colour and size. Then swap. Useful phrases: "Can I help you?", "I'm looking for ...", "Can I try it on?" Write 3 sentences: what costume you chose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for polite shop phrases and clothes and colour words. No prices are needed. Fast pairs can add a problem to solve, like the wrong size or no more pirate hats.

quests.title: Midsummer Beach Party
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Plan a Midsummer (Sant Joan) beach party, or another summer party you like, with two or three classmates. Agree on food, music and one fun activity. Useful phrases: "Let's ...", "What about ...?", "Good idea!" Write 3 sentences with "We are going to ..."
quests.teacherNote: Typical Sant Joan ideas in English are a bonfire, fireworks, sweet bread (coca) and music on the beach. Check that every member of the group suggests at least one idea.

quests.title: Hidden Holiday Word
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Find the hidden word! Use the first letter of each answer: a Saint George's Day present with pages (4 letters); opposite of "start" (3); month of Saint George's Day (5); a place with tents (4); where you stay in Pixel Plaza (5). Check with a classmate, then type the word.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: BEACH (book, end, April, camp, hotel). Fast finishers can write their own hidden-word puzzle for a classmate.

quests.title: Last Day of School
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Ask a partner about the last day of school before the summer holidays: "What did you do?", "How did you feel?", "What did you do after school?" Then answer their questions. Can't remember? Invent it! Useful phrases: "I felt ...", "We played ..." Write 3 sentences about your partner's day.
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple questions with "did" and irregular verbs (went, felt, ate). Near the end of the course, you can switch it to plans for this year's last day with "going to".

quests.title: Carnival Squad Costume
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Choose a group costume for the Carnival parade (or any costume party) with two or three classmates: one theme for everyone, like space, food or superheroes. Each person suggests a theme with a reason; compare them and vote. Then decide who wears what. Useful phrases: "I think ... would be better because ...", "That's funnier than ...", "What if we ...?" Write 4 sentences: your theme, why you chose it and each person's costume.
quests.teacherNote: Many Catalan towns and schools parade in group costumes, so students usually have real ideas. Listen for comparatives (funnier, easier to make) and reasons with "because"; if the vote is a tie, the group must find a compromise theme.

quests.title: Summer Camp Mystery
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Solve this puzzle with a partner. Ana, Biel, Carla and Dani go to four different summer camps: sailing, mountain, art and football. Each child goes to one camp. Dani needs a ball at his camp. Biel can't swim and he hates walking up hills. Ana feels sick in high places. Who goes to the sailing camp? Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "So ... must be at ..." Talk it through in the chat, then type only the name.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Ana. Dani needs a ball (football), so Biel, who can't swim and hates hills, must be at art camp; Ana avoids high places, so she takes sailing and Carla gets the mountain camp.

quests.title: Saint George's Book Hunt
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Get ready for Saint George's Day (Sant Jordi), when people give books and roses! Ask four classmates to recommend a book, comic or graphic novel, and ask follow-up questions. If the title isn't in English, describe the story instead. Then choose the one you most want to read. Useful phrases: "What's it about?", "It sounds more exciting than ...", "I'd love to read it because ..." Write 4 sentences: the recommendations you got and your choice, with a reason.
quests.teacherNote: The chat blocks words that are not English, so students describe books with Catalan or Spanish titles instead of typing them, which is good practice in explaining things another way. Any kind of reading counts, including comics.

quests.title: Spring or Summer Showdown
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Debate with a partner: which season is better, spring or summer? Compare the weather, food, free time and celebrations, like Saint George's Day or Midsummer. Ask "Why?" after every answer and try to agree on a winner. Useful phrases: "Spring is less ... than summer", "I prefer ... because ...", "That's true, but ..." Write 4 sentences: your partner's opinion, your opinion and your final decision.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives (warmer, less crowded, more relaxing) and reasons. If a pair agrees straight away, one student must defend the other season anyway.

quests.title: Mystery Postcard
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Write a postcard from your dream summer holiday: a beach, a camp, a city or your own town. Describe the weather, what you did yesterday and your plans for tomorrow, but don't name the place! Share it in the nearby chat and ask classmates to guess where you are. Useful phrases: "The weather here is ...", "Yesterday I ...", "Tomorrow I'm going to ..." Write your postcard (4-5 sentences) and say whether a classmate guessed it.
quests.teacherNote: Check the mix of tenses: past simple for yesterday and "going to" for tomorrow. Shy students can whisper the postcard to one classmate instead of posting it in the nearby chat.

quests.title: Beach Clean-Up Crew
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Imagine you and two or three classmates are organising a beach clean-up for the first Saturday of the summer holidays. Agree on a catchy slogan and three persuasive reasons to join. Then each of you tries to convince a classmate from another group to sign up, politely answering any excuses. Useful phrases: "Imagine how the beach would look if ...", "I see your point, but ...", "It only takes ..." Write a short paragraph: your slogan, your best arguments and how the persuading went.
quests.teacherNote: The classmates being persuaded can make up playful excuses to make it harder. In the paragraph, look for second conditionals and polite counter-arguments.

quests.title: The Holiday Compromise
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Plan an imaginary one-week summer trip with a partner, but you want different things. Decide who is A and who is B. A loves the beach, hates long walks and likes sleeping late. B loves the mountains, hates crowds and likes getting up early. Negotiate a plan you both accept: where you go, where you stay and what you do each day. Useful phrases: "I'd be happy to ... as long as ...", "How about a compromise?", "If we ..., then ..." Write a short paragraph summarising your plan and what each of you gave up.
quests.teacherNote: A good paragraph shows that both sides gave something up (e.g. a quiet beach campsite with one day in the mountains). For a harder version, add a twist: it rains for three days.

quests.title: The Long Summer Debate
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Survey at least four classmates: "Should summer holidays be shorter, with more short breaks during the school year?" Ask everyone for a reason, then test their opinion with a "what if" question, like "What if you had two extra weeks off in February?" Useful phrases: "Most people think ...", "Some argued that ..., while others ...", "Personally, I'm not convinced that ..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and your own opinion.
quests.teacherNote: This is a real debate in Catalonia, where summer holidays are long. Give credit to reports that sum up both sides fairly before giving their own view, and check reporting language (some argued that..., while others...).

quests.title: Midsummer Night Rules
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Run the Midsummer (Sant Joan) night party in Pixel Plaza with two or three classmates, or another summer festival you like. Some people want fireworks and loud music all night; others worry about noise, frightened pets and rubbish in the park. Agree on three rules that keep the party fun and fair for everyone. Useful phrases: "If we banned ..., people would ...", "On the other hand, ...", "A fair solution would be ..." Write a short paragraph: your three rules and the reasons behind them.
quests.teacherNote: Look for second conditionals and reasons that weigh both sides (fun against noise, pets and litter). Groups can post their rules in the nearby chat and the class can vote for the fairest set.

quests.title: The Dragon's Side
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Retell the Saint George's Day legend from the dragon's point of view. In the usual story, a knight defeats a dragon to save a princess and her town, and a red rose appears. But what if the dragon was misunderstood? Explain, as the dragon, what really happened and how you felt. Then share a short version in the chat and ask two classmates whether the dragon deserves a second chance. Useful phrases: "If only they had listened ...", "I had no choice but to ...", "Nobody ever asked why ..." Write a short paragraph as the dragon, plus one sentence about your classmates' verdict.
quests.teacherNote: Look for narrative tenses and ways of expressing regret (If only..., should have...). Keep it light and funny; the class can vote in the chat for the most convincing dragon.

quests.title: Twenty for the Café
quests.text: Find a classmate who is the café baker. Ask: "How many chestnuts does the café need?" If you are the baker, tell two classmates the answer: "The café needs ... chestnuts." Then type the number.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 20 (twenty). It comes from the Baker's reward for 'where' ("The café needs 20 chestnuts. That is half of the box."), so at least one baker must have answered 'where' before others can find it.

quests.title: No Chestnuts Today
quests.text: Invite three classmates to your café. Say: "Welcome! Sorry, we have no chestnuts today. Do you want hot chocolate, tea or cake?" Write 2 sentences: "... wants ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for bakers only, playing on the missing chestnuts. Check the third person -s in "wants"; stronger students can add "... doesn't want ..." or offer more café items.

quests.title: The Long Ride
quests.text: Find a classmate who is the driver. Ask: "How long is the ride from the shop to the park?" Then ask one more question. Are you the driver? Answer two classmates instead. Useful phrases: "How long does it take?" "It takes ..." Type the answer with a word like "minutes" or "hours".
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 30 minutes (half an hour), from the Driver's reward for 'where' ("The ride from the shop to the park takes 30 minutes."). A bare "30" is not accepted on purpose, because a wrong clock time like "9:30" would also match it.

quests.title: Morning in Town
quests.text: Interview four classmates: "Where were you in town at nine o'clock this morning? What did you see?" They can invent a fun answer about a normal morning. Useful phrases: "I was at the ...", "I saw ...". Write 3 sentences: who you asked and what they said.
quests.teacherNote: Answers are invented, so nobody shares real places, and the task is about witnesses, not suspects. Check was/were and past simple (saw, went); ask the class whether two people 'saw' the same thing.

quests.title: Lost Box Notice
quests.text: Write a "Lost box" notice in nearby chat. Say the box's colour, what is inside and when it left the shop. Ask three classmates: "Did you see this box?" Useful phrases: "Lost: a ... box with ...", "It left the shop at ...". Write 3 sentences: your notice and what two classmates said.
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for shopkeepers, built only on their starting clue (a blue box left the shop at 9:00) plus the obvious fact that it held chestnuts. Check that the notice is clear and that the replies they record use past simple.

quests.title: The Green Coat
quests.text: Talk to a hotel receptionist about the man in the green coat. Ask what he wanted and what time he came to the desk. Then ask a follow-up question, like "Why do you think he asked about the park?" Are you the receptionist? Answer a classmate's questions instead. Useful phrases: "What exactly did he ask?" "What makes you say that?" Type the time he asked about the park.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 9:15 (quarter past nine), from the Receptionist's reward for 'where' ("A man in a green coat asked me about the park at 9:15."). The 'coat' news says a neighbour saw a green coat near the park at 9:20, which is not accepted, so this is a good moment to compare the two times.

quests.title: Front Page News
quests.text: Work with two or three classmates as reporters for the town newspaper. Share what each of you knows about the missing chestnuts; report facts, not guesses. Everyone suggests a headline, then compare them and vote for the best one. Useful phrases: "I prefer ... because ...", "Yours is catchier than mine.", "Shall we choose ...?" Write the winning headline, 3 sentences of news and one reason why your group chose it.
quests.teacherNote: Works at any point in the chapter: early groups report what is still unknown, later groups can add the park and the times. Look for comparatives in the vote and check that the news contains facts, not accusations against classmates.

quests.title: Good News or Bad News?
quests.text: Go to the hotel and read the note on the door. Is it good news or bad news? Find a classmate who read it too and discuss it. Ask them a follow-up question. Useful phrases: "I think it's good news because...", "I'm not so sure, because...", "Why do you think that?" Write 3-4 sentences: your opinion, your partner's opinion and one reason for each.
quests.teacherNote: The hotel-door discovery says "The chestnuts are safe. Do not worry." Both readings (comforting or suspicious) are valid; reward clear because-clauses and real follow-up questions, not a 'right' opinion.

quests.title: Plan B for the Party
quests.text: Hold an emergency meeting with two or three classmates: the party starts at 6:00, you need the chestnuts before 5:00, and they are still not here. Propose two backup plans (for example, a different snack, a later start or a search team) and persuade the group to choose one. Listen to objections and negotiate a compromise. Useful phrases: "If we ..., we could ...", "I see your point, but ...", "What if we ...?" Write a short paragraph: the options, what each person thought and the final decision with reasons.
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for planners, built on the Planner's reward for 'where' (party at 6:00, chestnuts needed before 5:00). Look for conditionals, polite disagreement and a summary that includes the classmates' views, not only the planner's.

quests.title: Never Again Rules
quests.text: Meet two or three classmates and make next year's chestnut delivery safer: this year the lock was open and the box was empty! Each person suggests one rule about keys, locks, routes or times. Focus on rules, not on suspects. Discuss the pros and cons of every rule, then agree on the best two. Useful phrases: "If we had ..., this wouldn't have happened.", "The problem with that is ...", "On the other hand, ..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and your two final rules.
quests.teacherNote: Use after the chapter ending (two keys, open lock, empty box). Look for third conditionals and a summary that reports more than one view; the 'rules, not suspects' focus keeps the quest fair for every student, including a future thief.

quests.title: Follow the Blue Box
quests.text: Ask classmates: "Where is the blue box?" The driver knows. Then ask: "Where is the water in this town?" Type the place: "The box is near the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the pond in the park. It comes from the driver's starting clue ('I carried a blue box. I left it near the water.') plus the planner's starting clue ('The only water in town is the pond in the park.'). 'Water' or 'park' alone is not accepted, so students must ask both a driver and a planner.

quests.title: Clue Swap
quests.text: Find a classmate with a different job. Say: "I am the ... My clue is ..." Ask: "What is your job? What is your clue?" Write 1-2 sentences: "The ... says ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check that the student reports the partner's clue, not their own, e.g. 'The driver says the blue box is near the water.' Stronger A1 students can swap clues with two classmates. Remind them that some clues may not be true.

quests.title: Lost Chestnuts Poster
quests.text: Write a LOST notice for the festival chestnuts. Post it in the chat. Ask: "Did you see them?" Write 2 sentences here: "LOST: chestnuts! Please tell the ... at the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Good answers name a story job and a place, e.g. 'Please tell the baker at the cafe.' Faster students can add a detail from their clues, such as the blue box or a time. Replies in the chat are a bonus, not required.

quests.title: The Open Shop Door
quests.text: Find out why the shop door was open at 9:05. Ask a shopkeeper: "Where did you go at 9:05?" Then ask one more question, like "Why didn't you close the door?" Type the answer: "The shopkeeper went to the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the bank. It comes from the shopkeeper's reward for 'meet-shop' ('At 9:05 I went to the bank. The shop door was open.'). Shopkeepers only have this line after answering 'meet-shop' themselves, so if one has no answer, tell the student to ask another shopkeeper. The quest is hidden from shopkeepers because they cannot interview themselves.

quests.title: Hotel Phone Puzzle
quests.text: The hotel phone rang at 9:25 and nobody answered. Ask 3 classmates: "Did you call the hotel?" "Where were you at 9:25?" Write 3 sentences, one for each classmate: "My classmate ... was at/in the ... at 9:25." Only report what they say. Do not accuse anyone.
quests.teacherNote: Only receptionists see this. It builds on their starting clue ('The hotel phone rang at 9:25. Nobody answered.'). Look for correct 'was at/in' and past simple questions. The thief's cover story ('At 9:25 I was at the hotel desk') may appear; that is part of the game, and the quest never asks anyone to accuse a classmate.

quests.title: The Planner's Morning
quests.text: Interview a festival planner about their morning. Ask where they were at 9:20 and who was with them, then ask two follow-up questions, for example what they were doing and how the party plans are going now. Useful phrases: "Where exactly were you at 9:20?" "What were you doing there?" "How do you feel about the party now?" Type the place where the planner was at 9:20: "At 9:20 the planner was in the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the square. It comes from the planner's reward for 'meet-shop' ('At 9:20 I was in the square with the band'). 'Fountain' is also accepted because the fountain is in the square. A planner who has not answered 'meet-shop' yet will not have this line. Check the follow-up questions in the chat log, because they show more language than the one-word answer.

quests.title: The Driver's Delivery Log
quests.text: Prepare your secret delivery log. You carried a blue box and left it near the water, but the log needs more details. Ask a shopkeeper what time the box left the shop, ask classmates where the water is, and ask one more classmate what they saw that morning. Useful phrases: "What time did the box leave?" "Are you sure?" "What did you see?" Write 4-5 sentences in time order, then say which detail you are not sure about and why.
quests.teacherNote: Only drivers see this. A complete log includes 9:00 (shopkeeper's starting clue), the pond in the park (planner's starting clue) and one more witness detail, with sequencers like 'first', 'then', 'after that'. The 'not sure' sentence should give a reason.

quests.title: Breaking Festival News
quests.text: Report the festival morning for the town newspaper. Interview two classmates with different jobs: ask what they did or saw between 9:00 and 9:30, and ask each one a follow-up question. Report only what people said and do not accuse anyone. Useful phrases: "According to the baker, ..." "Both of them said ..." "Nobody knows yet why ..." Write a headline and 3-4 sentences: what each person said and whether their stories agree.
quests.teacherNote: Look for reporting verbs ('said', 'told me'), a short factual headline and a clear comparison of the two stories. If you have already shown the news, students can also mention that the shop door was open at 9:05 or that the hotel phone rang at 9:25.

quests.title: One Box, Two Stories
quests.text: Settle an argument between the cafe and the shop: they tell different stories about a blue box. Pair up with a classmate who has the other job (baker with shopkeeper) and compare your clues. Suggest at least two explanations that would make both of you right, then negotiate which is most likely. Useful phrases: "Suppose the box never..." "That would explain why..." "I'd accept that, as long as..." Write a short paragraph: both claims, your explanations, the one you agreed on and what you would ask the driver next.
quests.teacherNote: Only bakers and shopkeepers see this. Their starting clues are 'A blue box left the shop at 9:00' and 'No blue box came to the cafe'. A strong paragraph shows that both can be true, for example because the box went somewhere else (the driver left it near the water), and uses conditionals to compare the explanations.

quests.title: Why Take the Chestnuts?
quests.text: The chestnut mystery is solved, but one question is still open: why would someone take the festival chestnuts? With 2-3 classmates, suggest at least three possible motives for an imaginary thief, then challenge each other: which is most likely, and what evidence would you need? Then discuss how such a person could make things right before the party. Talk about a made-up character, never a real classmate. Useful phrases: "They might have wanted to..." "That seems unlikely because..." "If I were them, I would..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and the one your group finds most convincing.
quests.teacherNote: It unlocks after the chapter is solved and builds on the ending question ('But why did they take the chestnuts?'). The chapter does not answer it, so every idea is a guess. Look for modal speculation ('might have', 'can't have', 'must have') and a balanced summary. The thief is framed as an imaginary character so the student who played the thief is not singled out.

quests.title: The Heavy Bag
quests.text: Ask a driver: "What time does the heavy bag go to the hotel?" Say "Thank you!" Are you a driver? Ask another driver. Type the time.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 9:40. It comes from the driver's chapter 3 starting clue ("At 9:40 I carried a heavy bag to the hotel.") and the teacher news 'bag'. Digit and word forms are accepted (9:40, nine forty, twenty to ten).

quests.title: Truck Number Hunt
quests.text: Ask a driver: "What is the number of your truck?" The answer is: "My truck is number ..." It is part of the door code. Type the number. Are you a driver? Ask another driver.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 7. It is the driver's reward for 'hide' ("One number of the code is 7. It is the number of my truck."). A driver who has not answered 'hide' yet will not know it, so the student should try another driver. It gives only one digit, not the whole code.

quests.title: Haunted Party Snacks
quests.text: Help the town plan food for the haunted party. Ask three classmates: "What food do you like at a party?" Write two sentences, for example: "Leo likes pizza. Mia and Sam like hot chestnuts."
quests.teacherNote: Check the third-person -s (he likes, they like). Students who are stuck can use festival food such as hot chestnuts, sweet potatoes or cakes, or food from another celebration they like.

quests.title: Who Signed It?
quests.text: Ask a festival planner: "Who signed the note in the cellar?" Are you a planner? Ask another planner. Then ask someone with a different role: "What does your part of the note say?" Type who signed it: "A ... of the town."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: a friend of the town. It is the planner's reward for 'code' ("The note is signed by a friend of the town."). Any answer containing the word friend is accepted. A planner who has not answered 'code' yet will not know it, so the student should try another planner.

quests.title: Hotel Desk Survey
quests.text: Welcome four classmates to your hotel. Strange things are happening there! Ask each guest: "Did you see or smell anything strange near the hotel tonight?" Useful phrases: "Welcome to the hotel!", "Thank you for your help." Write 3 sentences: who you asked and what they said.
quests.teacherNote: Only receptionists see this. Look for past simple questions (Did you see...?) and short reported answers (She said she smelled chestnuts). Bakers and drivers have hotel clues, so they have something real to say.

quests.title: Town Gossip
quests.text: Share town gossip! Tell three classmates one thing from your role card. Listen to their news too. Useful phrases: "Did you hear about...?", "I heard that...", "Really? Who told you?" Write 3 sentences about what you heard, for example: "The shopkeeper told me that..."
quests.teacherNote: Good at the start of a session: each role has a different clue, so everyone hears something new. Look for "told me that" and "I heard that", and remind students to share hints, not answers. Students with the secret plan card can share a harmless hint.

quests.title: Secret Timeline
quests.text: Find a classmate with the other role (driver or shopkeeper) and send your clues to each other. Put the two events in time order. Then ask each other follow-up questions: what could be in the heavy bag, and why might somebody need fire? Useful phrases: "First..., then...", "It might mean that...", "I agree, but..." Write 3-5 sentences: your timeline and your theory.
quests.teacherNote: Only drivers and shopkeepers see this. Expected timeline: at 9:00 someone bought wood and matches (shopkeeper's clue), and at 9:40 a heavy bag went to the hotel (driver's clue). Good theories connect fire for roasting with the hotel and use might/could.

quests.title: Haunted Party Poster
quests.text: Work with two or three classmates to plan a poster for the haunted chestnut party. Ask a festival planner for the start time (planners: tell the others). Agree on a place in town, food, games and costumes, and add one idea from another celebration you like. Useful phrases: "What about...?", "I prefer... because...", "Let's go with..." Write the poster text in 3-5 sentences.
quests.teacherNote: The party starts at 6:00 (the planner's starting clue), so the best posters include that time. Look for suggestions with reasons. Groups can post their poster text in nearby chat and the class can vote.

quests.title: Plan B Party
quests.text: Save the party! It starts at 6:00 and the chestnuts are still missing. Persuade at least four classmates to help with a Plan B in case the chestnuts are not found in time. Listen to their ideas, answer their doubts and give each person a job, such as cooking, music or decorations. Useful phrases: "If we can't find them, we could...", "Would you be willing to...?", "I see your point, but..." Write a short paragraph: summarise the plan, who agreed to do what, and one objection you dealt with.
quests.teacherNote: Only festival planners see this. Look for conditionals and polite persuasion. A strong paragraph names at least three jobs and explains how one doubt was solved. If the class has already found the chestnuts, treat it as a backup plan for next year.

quests.title: Front Page Story
quests.text: Report the big story for the town newspaper! Interview two classmates with different roles: how did they help find the chestnuts, and was the surprise party plan a good idea? Call the person who hid the chestnuts "a friend of the town", not by name. Useful phrases: "According to...", "...explained that...", "while others felt that..." Write a headline and a short paragraph that summarises the night, quotes both people and compares their views.
quests.teacherNote: Use this after the chapter is solved. Check the reporting verbs and that both opinions appear. The "friend of the town" rule (from the signed note) keeps the student who played the thief from being singled out.

quests.title: Old Poster Time
quests.text: Walk to the park and read the old poster. What time is written on it? Type the time with numbers, like 4:15. Then tell a classmate: "The poster says ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer comes from the park discovery 'plan-old-poster': 5:00. This is the OLD draft time, not the real rehearsal time (5:30 in the hotel hall), so remind students it is crossed out. Students must walk into the park zone.

quests.title: Cold Night Clothes
quests.text: Ask two classmates: "What do you wear to a cold autumn party?" Write two sentences. Use this frame: "... wears ... to the party."
quests.teacherNote: Quick warm-up replacing a second food survey, to keep the batch varied. Check the sentences use 'wears' for one person. Students may talk about any celebration they like.

quests.title: Blue Box Time
quests.text: Find a classmate who is the Shopkeeper. Ask: "What time did the blue box leave the shop?" Type the time with numbers. Useful phrases: "Excuse me, are you the Shopkeeper?" "Thank you!"
quests.teacherNote: Answer is the Shopkeeper's role clue: 'A blue box left the shop at 9:00.' Needs at least one Shopkeeper in the class; if there is none, skip this quest.

quests.title: Party Snack Survey
quests.text: Secret mission for the Café baker: plan the party snack table. Ask three classmates: "What snack do you want at the party?" Choose three snacks for the table. Write three sentences: who you asked and which snacks you chose. Useful phrases: "Do you like ...?" "I want ..."
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for the Café baker only. Check that the student really asked three people and named three snacks. Any food is fine, including non-festival snacks.

quests.title: Breaking Town News
quests.text: The festival plan is missing! With two or three classmates, write one news headline and two sentences. Say what is missing, where you looked and what time the party starts. Useful phrases: "Where did you look?" "We looked in ..." "The party starts at ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for a headline plus two past-tense sentences. The party time is 6:00 (from the chapter intro). Students may guess where the plan is; that is fine.

quests.title: The Red Folder Trail
quests.text: Find the Café baker and interview them about the red folder. Ask at least two follow-up questions, for example: "What colour was it?" and "Who borrowed it?" Then type the job of the person who borrowed the folder. Useful phrases: "Could you tell me more about ...?" "What happened next?" "Did anyone else ...?"
quests.teacherNote: Answer comes from the Café baker's role clue: 'The planner borrowed my red folder.' The same clue mentions the hotel reception desk, so the quest unlocks only after the 'plan-location' answer. Listen for real follow-up questions; needs a Café baker in the class.

quests.title: Label That Box
quests.text: Secret mission for the Shopkeeper and the Driver: invent a label system for the boxes. Talk with the other role, or with any classmate. Decide four things to write on every label, for example colour and delivery time. Give reasons and ask follow-up questions. Write 3-5 sentences: the four things and why they help. Useful phrases: "I think we should write ... because ..." "What if ...?" "Good idea, but ..."
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for the Shopkeeper and the Driver. Look for four label items with a reason for each and some negotiation. Students can pair with any classmate if the other role is missing.

quests.title: What Happened Here?
quests.text: The festival plan has vanished! Ask four classmates what they think happened and what to do next. Ask follow-up questions. Do not accuse anyone: talk about ideas, not people. Write 3-5 sentences: what they said, which idea sounds most likely, and why. Useful phrases: "Why do you think so?" "Maybe it ..." "I agree because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check that students gather four different ideas and give a reason for their choice. Remind them to keep it kind and about the plan, not about classmates.

quests.title: Quiet Guest, Loud Party
quests.text: Secret mission for the Hotel receptionist and the Festival planner: a guest wants a quiet evening, but the neighbours want a lively party. Find two classmates and ask one to speak for the guest and one for the neighbours. Listen to both, summarise their views, propose a compromise and ask if they accept. Write a short paragraph: each view, your compromise, their answer, and what might happen if nobody gave way.
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for the Hotel receptionist and the Festival planner. Look for a fair summary of both views, a clear compromise and a hypothetical (what might happen if...). Check that the role-play stays kind.

quests.title: Outside or Inside?
quests.text: Hold a town meeting with three classmates. Should the Castanyada party, or another celebration you like, be outside in a park at night, or inside a large hall? Each person gives one advantage and one risk for each place. Use "If it rained ..." at least once. Write a short paragraph: the different views, your group's decision and your best reasons.
quests.teacherNote: Open debate that does not reveal the chapter's answer. Look for 'If it ... would ...' sentences, balanced summaries and a clear group decision.

quests.title: Lantern Picture Clue
quests.text: Find the picture on the missing lantern. Ask classmates: "What is on the lantern?" Type the answer in one or two words.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: moon. It comes from the Festival planner's starting clue ("The lantern has a moon on it"), so students without that role must ask. If nobody knows yet, suggest asking more classmates.

quests.title: Baker's Menu Mission
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "What food do you like at a celebration?" Then write 2 sentences: "Most classmates like ... . As the baker, I will make ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for the Cafe baker. Check that the sentences use the frame and name real foods from classmates. Any celebration food is fine, not only chestnuts.

quests.title: Design a Lantern
quests.text: Imagine your own festival lantern. Tell a classmate about it. Ask: "What is on your lantern?" Then write 2 sentences: "My lantern is ... . It has a ... ." Example: "My lantern is red. It has a star."
quests.teacherNote: Creative warm-up, no drawing needed. Look for colour and object words and 'has a'. Students may design a decoration for another celebration instead.

quests.title: Free Chestnuts
quests.text: Read the invitation at the hotel, or ask a classmate what it says. Which food is free at the celebration? Ask your partner: "Do you like it?" Type the free food.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: chestnuts. Source: hotel discovery (the moon invitation says "Free chestnuts, optional costumes and activities"). Gated after the special-guests objective because the invitation also reveals who the welcome is for.

quests.title: Strange Sound Survey
quests.text: Imagine you hear a strange sound in the park at night. Ask two classmates: "What are you going to do?" Write 3 sentences. Useful phrases: "I am going to ..." "Maybe it is ..." "My classmate is going to ..."
quests.teacherNote: Light spooky fun that does not reveal the cause of the sound. Check going to and maybe, and that students report classmates' answers kindly without embarrassing anyone.

quests.title: How Many Newcomers
quests.text: Your team knows who the welcome is for. Now find the number. Ask classmates: "How many new neighbors are in town?" Some classmates have a number in their notes. Ask follow-up questions and compare answers. Useful phrases: "How do you know?" "Are you sure?" "Thank you, that helps." Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: ten. Source: the Driver's and Receptionist's rewards for the sound objective (ten new neighbors), also in the guests news. Baker, Shopkeeper and Planner must ask, which creates the information gap.

quests.title: Clear Directions Mission
quests.text: Give a classmate directions from the hotel hall entrance to the food table. Invent the route, but keep the words short and clear. Ask your partner to repeat the route and say: "Is it clear?" Then write 3-5 sentences: your directions, what your partner understood and one thing you changed. Useful phrases: "Go straight..." "Turn left at..." "It is next to..."
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for the Driver, linked to the Driver's welcome requirement (clear directions). The route can be invented; look for direction phrases and a real revision after feedback.

quests.title: Town News Report
quests.text: Write a short town newspaper report about the missing lantern and the ghostly sound. Choose a headline, then ask a classmate to read it and say what is unclear. Write 3-5 sentences: your headline, the main facts and one change after your partner's feedback. Useful phrases: "According to ..." "Because of the wind ..." "Could you make it clearer?"
quests.teacherNote: Gated after the sound is explained so the report can mention wind. Look for facts from the clues, a clear headline and a real revision.

quests.title: Newcomer Welcome Plan
quests.text: Find a classmate with the other role. Together, plan a short welcome for a newcomer who knows nothing about Castanyada (or another celebration you like). Shopkeeper: explain what happens and why, without assuming anything is known. Receptionist: suggest how to offer company without forcing anyone to join. Argue for your best ideas, agree on a plan and write one paragraph: the explanation, the offer of company and why newcomers would feel comfortable.
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for the Shopkeeper and Hotel receptionist, based on their welcome notes. If no partner has the other role, two students can swap roles. Look for explanation without assumed knowledge and real choice for guests.

quests.title: Costumes Or Not
quests.text: Discuss with two or three classmates: should costumes be optional, encouraged, or banned at a welcome celebration? Ask everyone for an opinion and a reason, and try to persuade each other politely. Then write a short paragraph summarising the different views, saying which one the group chose and what compromise (if any) helped. You can use another celebration you like as an example.
quests.teacherNote: Gated after the ending because the invitation says costumes are optional. Look for balanced summaries, polite persuasion and respect for students who prefer not to dress up.
